Mark as read Big picture How the test works Mark difficult Aspect What to expect Where Electronically on **Remindo**, **on premises** — it cannot be taken from home Duration Depends on the number of questions, often around **2 hours** Allowed material **None**: no books, notes or other material Question kinds (i) **Multiple choice**; (ii) **free answer** (text) — including a few **programming** questions where only a small part of a program is written, in **pseudocode** (not real code) Parts **Theory** (the lectures) and the **practical assignment** Weight The final test counts for 40% of the grade, the project for 60% (Lecture 1) Style No fixed rule for the number or type of questions; this course typically uses the two kinds above The final test at a glance, from the course's exam information. Points follow effort. In the style of the sample test, a one-line multiple-choice question is worth about 0.5 point , an explain or what is the difference question about 1.5 points , and a MapReduce design question several points. Plan your time accordingly: do not spend ten minutes on a half-point question, and leave enough time for the pseudocode question. A time plan for two hours 1 First pass (≈ 40 min) Answer every multiple-choice and short question you are sure of. Mark the rest. Reveal step 2 of 4 Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. What two kinds of questions does this course's test use? Show answer What are the two parts of the test? Show answer What material may you bring? Show answer Mark as read Worked examples Writing answers that score Mark difficult The test instructions are clear: stay to the point and give what the question asks ; avoid material that was not asked — every question can be fully answered with a short, precise answer. Extra paragraphs do not earn points, and a wrong extra claim can cost them. Use these templates: Question asks… Answer with… Length “What is X?” / “Explain X” Definition in one sentence · what it is for · its key property or mechanism · one example 3–5 sentences “Difference between X and Y?” / “Are they the same?” What X is · what Y is · the key difference (often: purpose, or where/how) · an example of each if asked 4–6 sentences “Advantages and disadvantages” Two or three bullets each, for **each** option asked about Bullets “Why…?” The cause, then the consequence — one chain of reasoning 2–3 sentences “Write the map and reduce…” Signatures with types, the key choice, what map emits, what reduce receives and emits; a two-line trace helps Pseudocode + 1–2 sentences A calculation The formula, the substituted numbers, the result with its unit A few lines Worked example: “Explain what an RDD is.” 1 Weak answer “RDD is a Spark thing for data that is fast because it is in memory and it is resilient and you can do map and filter on it and it was invented at Berkeley…” — vague, and drifts off topic. Reveal step 2 of 2 Worked example: “Write the map and the reduce function that compute the sum of n integers.” 1 Choose the key All integers must meet in one reducer, so every map output uses the same constant key , e.g. "sum". Reveal step 2 of 4 Multiple-choice tactics Read the stem twice: “which is NOT” questions catch fast readers. Eliminate options that are true but answer another question (e.g. “to make things run faster on the machine” is not the purpose of MapReduce — scaling out is). Be suspicious of absolutes ( always, only, never ) and of options that are half right. When two options look equal, choose the one that names the mechanism (lineage, quorum overlap, index-free adjacency) rather than a vague benefit. Graph query languages beyond Cypher A question can also name languages that are only mentioned in passing. Cypher is Neo4j's declarative, pattern-matching graph query language (Lecture 11). PGQL (Oracle) and G-CORE (a proposal by the LDBC working group) are other declarative query languages for property graphs , in the same ASCII-art pattern style — the line of work that led to the ISO GQL standard. Knowing that all three are property-graph query languages is the core of the answer. Mark as read Core concepts Comparisons the test likes Mark difficult Difference between X and Y is the most common open question. Each row below is the core of a full-marks answer — expand it with a definition of each side and an example. X vs Y Key difference Lecture Hadoop vs HDFS Hadoop is the whole ecosystem (MapReduce computation + HDFS storage + tools); HDFS is only its distributed file system 8, 9 Spark vs Hadoop MapReduce Spark keeps intermediate data in memory (RDDs, lineage) and has a richer API; MapReduce writes to HDFS between every job — slow for iterative and interactive work 8 Transformation vs action Transformations (map, filter) return a new RDD lazily; actions (count, collect) return a value and trigger execution 8 Combiner vs reducer A combiner pre-aggregates map output locally, before the shuffle, and only works for associative and commutative functions; the reducer produces the final result per key 7 Graph DB vs graph analytics A graph database stores and queries graphs (Neo4j: find friends of friends); graph analytics processes whole graphs (centrality, k-core, PageRank) 11 Graph DB vs relational DB for graphs Graph DB: index-free adjacency, cheap traversals, flexible schema, natural modelling; but hard to shard. Relational: mature, SQL, scales and optimises well; but traversals need many (self-)joins 11 Native vs non-native graph processing Native: each node points to its neighbours (O(1) per hop); non-native: hops go through a global index (O(log n)) 11 CREATE vs MERGE CREATE always adds; MERGE adds only the parts of a pattern that are missing 11 Key-value vs document store Both store aggregates by key; a key-value value is opaque, a document's structure is visible, so you can query and index inside it 10 Column-family vs relational table Column families group columns accessed together; rows can have different columns; no joins — model for the queries 10 ACID vs BASE ACID: atomic, consistent, isolated, durable transactions; BASE: basically available, soft state, eventually consistent — availability and speed over immediate consistency 1, 3, 10 CP vs AP (CAP) Under a partition, CP refuses requests to stay consistent; AP stays available and reconciles later 3, 10 Horizontal vs vertical fragmentation Horizontal splits rows by a predicate (union reconstructs); vertical splits columns, each fragment keeps the key (join reconstructs) 3 Replication vs fragmentation Replication copies the same data to several sites (availability, read speed); fragmentation splits data so each site holds a part (locality, parallelism) 3 Static vs extendible vs linear hashing Static: fixed buckets, overflow chains; extendible: a directory that doubles, split only the full bucket; linear: no directory, buckets split in round-robin order 1 Hash index vs B+ tree Hash: equality only, O(1); B+ tree: equality and ranges, sorted, O(log n) 1 Shingling vs minhashing vs LSH Shingling: documents → sets; minhashing: sets → short signatures preserving Jaccard; LSH: signatures → candidate pairs 5, 6 Jaccard vs cosine Jaccard compares sets (intersection over union); cosine compares vectors by angle 2, 12 GFS vs HDFS terms Master ↔ NameNode, chunkserver ↔ DataNode, chunk (64 MB) ↔ block, operation log ↔ EditLog, checkpoint ↔ FsImage 9 k-NN vs ANN k-NN: the exact k nearest; ANN: k vectors almost as near (within c × the best), much faster with an index 12 Pre- vs post-filtering Pre: filter on attributes, then search (k results); post: search, then filter (may return fewer than k) 12 Vector DB vs relational DB Vector DB stores high-dimensional vectors and answers similarity (ranking) queries with special indexes; From the database textbook: how to use the principle of a hash function in different scenarios, what a hash index is and how it works; the difference with the B+ tree index, how the latter works, and what benefits it brings. TF.IDF (MMDS 1.3.1) Mark as known Finds the words that characterise a document: frequent in this document , rare in the collection . TF ᵢⱼ = fᵢⱼ / maxₖ fₖⱼ — frequency of word i in document j, divided by the frequency of the most frequent word in j. IDF ᵢ = log₂(N / nᵢ) — N documents in total, nᵢ of them contain word i. Score = TF × IDF. A word in every document has IDF = log₂ 1 = 0. Stop words score low, topic words high. Hash functions (MMDS 1.3.2) Mark as known A hash function h maps a hash-key to a bucket number 0 … B−1 and should spread the keys evenly ("randomise" them). Integers: h(x) = x mod B. Choose B prime : if B shares a factor with the keys (all keys even, B = 10) only some buckets are used. Strings and other types: convert to an integer first (e.g. sum the character codes, or group characters), then mod B. Records: combine the hashes of the components. Uses in this course: hash indexes, grouping keys in MapReduce (which reducer gets a key), sharding and partitioning, hashed shingles, minhashing, LSH buckets, Bloom filters. Indexes and secondary storage (MMDS 1.3.3–1.3.4) Mark as known An index is a data structure that retrieves records efficiently given the value of one or more fields, without scanning everything. A hash table is one way: hash the field value, look only in that bucket. Disks are organised in blocks (e.g. 64 KB). Reading a block takes about 10 ms — roughly 10⁵ times slower than main memory. So an algorithm's cost is counted in disk I/Os (blocks read), and good algorithms keep the data they need in memory or read each block once. Hash index: static, extendible, linear Mark as known A hash index puts each data entry in the bucket h(key). Equality search ≈ 1–2 I/Os. No range queries — hashing destroys order. Static hashing: a fixed number of primary pages; full buckets get overflow chains , which grow long as the file grows. Extendible hashing: a directory of 2ᵈ pointers (d = global depth , the last d bits of h); each bucket has a local depth l. When a bucket overflows: split only that bucket ; if l = d the directory doubles first. Costs at most one extra I/O for the directory. Linear hashing: no directory . Buckets are split in round-robin order (pointer Next ), whichever bucket overflowed; hash family hᵢ(v) = h(v) mod 2ⁱN. If hᵢ(v) points before Next , use hᵢ₊₁. Overflow pages exist, but only briefly. B+ tree: how it works Mark as known A balanced tree: every root-to-leaf path has the same length. Index (inner) nodes hold only keys and pointers to direct the search. Leaves hold the data entries and are chained to their neighbours. Order d: every node holds between d and 2d entries (the root: 1 to 2d), so it is always at least half full. Fan-out is large (≈ 100+), so the height ≈ log_fanout(N) is 3–4 in practice. Search: root to leaf, one page per level. Insert: into the right leaf. If full, split : in a leaf the middle key is copied up (it stays in the leaf); in an index node it is pushed up (it moves). Splits can cascade to the root, which is how the tree grows taller. Delete: if a node falls below d entries, redistribute from a sibling, otherwise merge with it (and remove the separator in the parent). Hash index versus B+ tree, and the B+ tree's benefits Mark as known Hash index B+ tree Equality (key = v) ≈ 1–2 I/Os — best height of the tree (3–4 I/Os) Range (a ≤ key ≤ b) not supported find a, then follow the leaf chain Sorted output, prefix search, min/max no yes Growth directory doubling / splitting stays balanced automatically Benefits of the B+ tree: supports equality and range queries, keeps the data sorted, stays balanced under inserts and deletes with a guaranteed log cost, and nodes are always at least 50% full. A clustered index (data stored in key order) makes ranges read few pages; an unclustered one may cost one I/O per matching record. Lectures 2, 5 and 6 8 of 8 to study Part 1 in full Part 2 in full Part 3 in full Entity resolution and finding similar items I know all of this What the course says is expected What entity resolution is, why we need it, at what level it can occur, the different distance metrics, in what situations they are used, and their formulas. How to generate n-grams, perform min-hash and apply LSH. MMDS Chapter 3: 3.1.1 to 3.4, 3.5, 3.8.1, 3.8.2 and 3.8.3. What a distance metric is and the popular distance metrics. Entity resolution: what, why, at which levels Mark as known What: deciding whether two descriptions (records, data structures) refer to the same real-world entity — then identifying them, deciding how to merge, and updating the collection. Also called deduplication, record linkage, entity linkage. Why needed: the same entity appears differently because of text variations — misspellings, acronyms, abbreviations, different word order, transformations; local knowledge — every source has its own formats and identifiers; there is no global coordination. Without it, integrated data has duplicates and wrong counts and joins. Levels (families of solutions): Atomic values — compare strings (edit distance, Jaro…). Sets — compare records as sets of values or tokens (Jaccard). Inner relationships — use the links between entities (co-authors separate the different "Ling Chen"). Uncertain data — keep probabilities instead of forcing a decision. Cost: N records give N(N−1)/2 pairs (10⁶ records ≈ 5·10¹¹), so comparing everything is infeasible → blocking, minhashing, LSH. String measures: edit, gap, Jaro, Jaro-Winkler Mark as known Edit distance (Levenshtein): minimum number of inserts, deletes and substitutions to turn x into y. MMDS version (inserts and deletes only): |x| + |y| − 2·|LCS(x, y)| . Use: typos in strings. Gap (affine gap) distance: a run of missing characters costs an opening cost plus a small extension cost per character, so long gaps are cheap. Use: abbreviations ("knowl. data"). Jaro similarity: ⅓·(C/|s₁| + C/|s₂| + (C − T)/C) , with C = common characters (within half the longer length) and T = transpositions (half the common characters out of order). Use: short strings, names . Jaro-Winkler: Jaro plus a bonus for a common prefix — names usually agree at the start. What a distance metric is (MMDS 3.5.1) Mark as known A function d(x, y) producing a number, with four axioms : d(x, y) ≥ 0 — no negative distances; d(x, y) = 0 if and only if x = y ; d(x, y) = d(y, x) — symmetry; d(x, y) ≤ d(x, z) + d(z, y) — the triangle inequality. Euclidean spaces have points with real coordinates (an average of points exists). Non-Euclidean spaces (sets, strings) do not. The popular distance measures, formula and use Mark as known Measure Formula Use for Euclidean L₂ √Σ(xᵢ − yᵢ)² points in space Manhattan L₁ Σ|xᵢ − yᵢ| grid-like differences L∞ max |xᵢ − yᵢ| largest single difference Lᵣ norm (Σ|xᵢ − yᵢ|ʳ)^(1/r) the general form Jaccard distance 1 − |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| sets (shingles, purchases) Cosine distance the angle arccos(x·y / (‖x‖·‖y‖)) vectors where only direction matters (text, embeddings) Edit distance inserts + deletes (+ substitutions) strings Hamming distance number of positions that differ bit vectors of equal length Example: a = (5, 5), b = (9, 8): L₂ = 5, L₁ = 7, L∞ = 4. Generating n-grams (k-shingles) (MMDS 3.2) Mark as known A k-shingle (character n-gram) is any substring of length k. A document becomes the set of its k-shingles, so documents sharing text share shingles. "abcdabd", k = 2 → {ab, bc, cd, da, bd} (ab appears twice, counted once). A document of n characters has at most n − k + 1 shingles. Choosing k: large enough that any given shingle is unlikely in any given document: k ≈ 5 for short texts (emails), k ≈ 9–10 for long documents. Too small (k = 1) → every document looks similar. Hashed shingles: hash 9-shingles to 4-byte integers — more discriminating than 4-shingles in the same space. Word shingles: e.g. a stop word followed by the next two words — favours the article text over page clutter. Similarity of two documents = Jaccard similarity of their shingle sets. For bags : intersection counts min, union counts the sum. Performing minhash (MMDS 3.3) Mark as known Goal: replace large sets by short signatures that preserve Jaccard similarity. Characteristic matrix: rows = elements (shingles), columns = sets, 1 if the element is in the set. For two columns, with a = rows (1,1) and b, c = rows with exactly one 1: SIM = a / (a + b + c) . Minhash of a column under a random permutation of the rows = the first row (in permuted order) where the column has a 1. Key property: P[h(C₁) = h(C₂)] = SIM(C₁, C₂) . Signature = the minhash values under n permutations. Signature similarity = fraction of positions that agree ≈ Jaccard similarity (more hash functions → smaller error). In practice (row hashing instead of permutations): Pick n hash functions hᵢ(r) on row numbers; set every SIG(i, c) = ∞. For each row r: compute h₁(r) … hₙ(r) once. For each column c with a 1 in row r: SIG(i, c) = min (SIG(i, c), hᵢ(r)). Applying LSH: banding and the S-curve (MMDS 3.4) Mark as known Goal: find candidate pairs without comparing all pairs of signatures. Split the signature matrix into b bands of r rows (n = b·r). Hash each band's portion of every column to buckets. Two columns are a candidate pair if they land in the same bucket for at least one band . For a pair with similarity s: P[candidate] = 1 − (1 − sʳ)ᵇ — an S-curve . Threshold (where it rises steeply) ≈ (1/b)^(1/r) . More rows per band (fewer bands) → threshold moves up : fewer false positives, more false negatives. More bands → the opposite. False positive: dissimilar pair that becomes a candidate (costs a check). False negative: similar pair never becoming a candidate (lost). Example: b = 20, r = 5: s = 0.8 → 0.9996; s = 0.3 → 0.047; threshold ≈ 0.55. Whole pipeline: shingle → minhash signatures → choose b, r for the target threshold → LSH gives candidates → check the signatures (and optionally the documents) of candidates. LSH for entity resolution and validating matches (MMDS 3.8.1–3.8.3) Mark as known Records, not documents: records have fields, so score each field (e.g. with edit distance) and add the scores; a pair above a threshold is a match. Avoiding all pairs: instead of minhashing, use simple "hash functions" on fields — put records in the same bucket if they agree exactly on a field (name, or address, or phone); only records sharing a bucket are scored. This is blocking . Validating without labelled data: use a field not used in the score (e.g. a creation date). For true matches the dates should be close; for random pairs they differ by a known average. If random pairs differ by 45 on average, true matches by 10, and the candidates' average is x, the fraction of true matches is f = (45 − x) / 35 . Any field that true matches agree on (and false ones do not) can validate the method the same way. Lecture 3 7 of 7 to study Lecture 3 in full Distributed databases I know all of this What the course says is expected Understand and use horizontal and vertical fragmentation, and how to combine the fragments into the complete dataset. Know the concepts of sharding, data transparency, optimization, replication, the quorum consensus protocol, two-phase commit, joins with regular or Bloom filters, Greenplum (what it is and a fragmentation example) and MemSQL. Relational algebra, ER and SQL are assumed. Horizontal and vertical fragmentation, and reconstruction Mark as known Horizontal: split the tuples with selections — Rᵢ = σ_pᵢ(R). Reconstruct with union: R = R₁ ∪ R₂ ∪ … With n decomposition predicates you get up to 2ⁿ fragments (all combinations of pᵢ / ¬pᵢ). Vertical: split the attributes with projections — Rᵢ = π_Aᵢ(R). Every fragment must contain the key (or a tuple id). Reconstruct with a join on the key: R = R₁ ⋈ R₂ ⋈ … Combined: fragment one way, then the other; reconstruct in reverse order. Correctness rules: completeness (every tuple / attribute is in some fragment), reconstructability (R can be rebuilt), disjointness (no data in two fragments — optional; given up on purpose for replication, and the key always repeats in vertical fragments). Derived horizontal fragmentation: fragment a second relation to follow the first using a semi-join (Lectures ⋉ Professorsᵢ), so each join can be done locally. Sharding, allocation and data transparency Mark as known Sharding = horizontal fragmentation across machines by a shard key (hash or range); each node stores one shard. Gives scale-out and parallelism. Allocation = deciding which fragment is stored on which site — without replication (each fragment once) or with replication (some fragments on several sites). Transparency = what the user does not need to know: Fragmentation transparency — query the global relation as if it were not fragmented (the highest level); Replication transparency — unaware that copies exist; Location transparency — unaware of which site holds the data. Query translation and optimization Mark as known Translate: replace each global relation by its reconstruction (∪ of horizontal fragments, ⋈ of vertical ones) — the naive plan ships everything and rebuilds the relations. Optimize: push selections and projections down into the fragments; drop fragments whose predicate contradicts the query (a selection on rank = C4 never needs the fragment of other ranks); with derived fragmentation, push the join below the union so each site joins locally and only small results are unioned. Goal: ship as little data as possible and do work in parallel at the sites. Replication and the quorum consensus protocol Mark as known Replication: several sites hold copies → faster reads, availability, locality. Price: keeping copies consistent on writes. ROWA (read one, write all): cheap reads; a write fails if any replica is down. Quorum consensus: each site has a weight ; W = total weight. Choose a read quorum Qr and a write quorum Qw with Qr + Qw > W — every read overlaps the latest write; 2·Qw > W — two writes cannot happen at once. A read locks sites of total weight ≥ Qr and takes the copy with the highest version number . A write locks ≥ Qw and increases the version. Example: weights 3, 1, 2, 2 → W = 8; Qw = 5, Qr = 4 is valid. ROWA is Qw = W, Qr = 1. Two-phase commit Mark as known Makes a transaction over several sites atomic (all commit or all abort). Roles: one coordinator , several agents (participants). Phase 1 – voting: coordinator sends PREPARE . Each agent writes its changes to its log and answers READY (it can commit) or FAILED . Phase 2 – decision: all READY → coordinator logs and sends COMMIT ; otherwise ABORT . Agents act and send ACK . Blocking problem: an agent that answered READY may neither commit nor abort by itself. If the coordinator crashes before sending the decision, the agents wait — holding their locks — until it recovers. The coordinator is a single point of failure (hence 3PC, Paxos, Raft). Distributed joins: semi-join and Bloom filter Mark as known Joining R (site 1) with S (site 2) on attribute C without shipping a whole relation: Semi-join filter: send only π_C(R) to site 2; compute S′ = S ⋉ R there (the S tuples that have a partner); ship S′ back and join. R ⋈ S = R ⋈ (S ⋉ π_C(R)). Pays off when few tuples have partners. Bloom filter: instead of the values, send a bit vector of m bits: for every join value of R set the bits h₁(v) … h_k(v). Site 2 keeps only S tuples whose bits are all set. Much smaller message, but false positives ("false drops") — some non-matching tuples are shipped and then removed by the real join. Never false negatives. By data placement: co-located join (both tables sharded on the join key → local joins, no shipping), broadcast join (small table copied to every node), distributed / redistribute join (reshuffle one side on the join key). Greenplum and MemSQL Mark as known Greenplum: a massively parallel (MPP), shared-nothing database built on PostgreSQL. A master plans queries; segments store the data and execute in parallel. DISTRIBUTED BY (col) — hash-shards rows across segments (horizontal fragmentation between nodes). DISTRIBUTED RANDOMLY = round-robin. PARTITION BY RANGE / LIST — splits a table within each segment (e.g. one partition per month), so queries skip partitions. Example: sales DISTRIBUTED BY (trans_id) PARTITION BY RANGE (date) with sub-partitions by region. MemSQL (SingleStore): a distributed in-memory SQL database. Aggregator nodes route and combine; leaf nodes store shards. Tables are sharded by a SHARD KEY ; small reference tables are replicated to every node so joins with them are local. Lecture 4 2 of 2 to study Lecture 4 in full In-database machine learning I know all of this What the course says is expected Know the idea of in-database machine learning and its benefits: running machine learning directly where the data is stored, rather than extracting it into the memory of another system. Depending on the database, it may support training models, making predictions, or both. The idea Mark as known In-database machine learning = running machine learning where the data is stored , instead of exporting the data to a separate ML system and loading it into that system's memory. Depending on the database it supports training , prediction (scoring) , or both . How it is possible: SQL can iterate with recursive queries (k-means, gradient descent), matrices can be stored as (i, j, value) relations and multiplied with a join + SUM … GROUP BY, and some systems add arrays and automatic differentiation. The six benefits Mark as known Less data movement — no copying of large datasets to an ML platform: saves transfer time and duplicate storage. Fresher predictions — models work on the current records, not on a periodic export. Simpler workflows — preparation and prediction fit into existing SQL queries, reports and applications; fewer pipelines to maintain. Easier access for analysts — people who know SQL can use ML without building a Python application. More centralised security — no exported copies; the database's access control and auditing are reused. Efficient processing at scale — uses the database's parallel processing ; no need to pull everything onto one machine. Example: an online store scores each customer's likelihood of leaving and joins the predictions with the customer records to produce a retention report — all inside the database. Lecture 7 6 of 6 to study Lecture 7 in full MapReduce I know all of this What the course says is expected Know what MapReduce is and be able to write a MapReduce program for some basic sequential tasks. Study material: MMDS Chapter 2. It is very important to know the examples of that chapter: how to create an inverted index, how to multiply matrices, and how to make joins. What MapReduce is Mark as known A programming model and system for processing very large data in parallel on a cluster of commodity machines, tolerating failures . Purpose: distribute and scale out (almost) linearly . You write two functions; the system does the rest. map(in_key, in_value) → list(out_key, intermediate_value) — applied to every input element independently. Group by key (shuffle) — the system collects all values of the same key; a hash of the key decides the reducer, so each key goes to exactly one reducer . reduce(out_key, list(intermediate_value)) → list(out_value) — combines all values of one key. Combiner: runs the reduce function inside the map task before the shuffle; allowed only if it is associative and commutative (sum, max — not average). Flow: Map → Combine → Reduce . Reduce can start only when all mappers have finished . How a job runs and survives failures Mark as known Input files live in a distributed file system, split into chunks . The master creates M map tasks (one per chunk) and R reduce tasks and assigns them to workers . Map output is written to the map worker's local disk , partitioned into R files; reduce workers fetch, sort, and reduce; the output goes to the DFS. Map worker fails: redo all its map tasks, even completed ones (their output was local and is gone). Reduce worker fails: reschedule only its running tasks (finished output is already in the DFS). Master fails: the whole job restarts. Writing basic programs: the recipe and the standard ones Mark as known Recipe: decide what must meet in one reducer → make that the key . Task map emits reduce does Word count (word, 1) sum Sum of n integers ("sum", x) — one constant key sum Max / min per group (group, value) max / min Average per group (group, (value, 1)) sum both, divide ( not an average of averages) Selection σ (t, t) if the condition holds identity Projection π (t′, t′) emit once (removes duplicates) Union (t, t) emit once Intersection (t, t) emit if both relations sent it Difference R − S (t, "R") or (t, "S") emit if only "R" Group by A, aggregate θ(B) (a, b) apply θ Example: inverted index Mark as known For every word, the list of documents that contain it. map(docId, text): for each word w in the text → emit (w, docId) . reduce(w, list of docIds): emit (w, sorted list of distinct docIds) . Example: natural join R(A, B) ⋈ S(B, C) Mark as known map: tuple (a, b) of R → emit (b, ("R", a)) ; tuple (b, c) of S → emit (b, ("S", c)) . The join attribute is the key ; the tag says which relation the value came from. reduce(b, list): separate the R-values and the S-values; for every pair (a from R, c from S) emit (a, b, c) . Input is a set of files with tuples of both relations: the in_key is the position / file, the in_value is one tuple with its relation name. Example: matrix-vector and matrix multiplication Mark as known Matrices are stored as triples (i, j, mᵢⱼ). Matrix × vector x = M·v (v fits in memory): map (i, j, mᵢⱼ) → (i, mᵢⱼ·vⱼ) ; reduce: sum → xᵢ. If v does not fit, cut M and v into matching stripes. Matrix × matrix P = M·N, two jobs: map: mᵢⱼ → (j, (M, i, mᵢⱼ)); nⱼₖ → (j, (N, k, nⱼₖ)). reduce on j: for each pair emit ((i, k), mᵢⱼ·nⱼₖ) — a join on j . map: identity. reduce on (i, k): sum → pᵢₖ. One job: map: mᵢⱼ → ((i, k), (M, j, mᵢⱼ)) for every k ; nⱼₖ → ((i, k), (N, j, nⱼₖ)) for every i . reduce on (i, k): match the values with the same j, multiply, sum . Lecture 8 4 of 4 to study Lecture 8 in full Apache Spark I know all of this What the course says is expected Spark versus Hadoop (what is the difference), how Spark operates, what RDDs are, what DataFrames are, and how they are used. Spark versus Hadoop Mark as known Hadoop = an ecosystem: MapReduce (computation) + HDFS (storage) + YARN, Hive, HBase… (So HDFS is one part of Hadoop.) Hadoop MapReduce writes to and reads from disk (HDFS) between every job — replication, serialisation, I/O — so it is slow for iterative algorithms (machine learning) and interactive queries; code is verbose; no real-time processing. Spark = a general-purpose cluster processing framework (not storage — it reads HDFS, S3, databases…). Hadoop MapReduce Spark Intermediate data on disk (HDFS) in memory (cacheable) Iterative / interactive slow fast (10–100×) Fault tolerance replication, re-run tasks lineage : recompute lost partitions API map and reduce only many operators; SQL, streaming, MLlib, GraphX Languages mainly Java Scala, Java, Python, R How Spark operates Mark as known The driver program holds the SparkContext (SparkSession), turns your code into a DAG of operations, and schedules tasks . A cluster manager (standalone, YARN, Mesos, Kubernetes) allocates worker nodes . Executors on the workers run the tasks and cache data; results return to the driver. Lazy evaluation: transformations only build the DAG (the lineage ). An action triggers execution of everything needed. Without cache() / persist() , every action recomputes the whole chain from the source; persisting keeps an RDD in memory (or disk) for reuse. Data is split into partitions (about 2–4 per CPU); one task per partition. RDDs and how they are used Mark as known RDD = Resilient Distributed Dataset: an immutable , partitioned collection of records distributed over the cluster, lazily evaluated , cacheable , and fault-tolerant through lineage (a lost partition is recomputed from its parents — no replication needed). Create: from a collection (parallelize) or external data (textFile on HDFS, S3…), or from another RDD. Transformations (lazy, return an RDD): map, filter, flatMap, distinct, union, intersection, subtract, cartesian, reduceByKey, groupByKey, join. Actions (return a value to the driver, trigger computation): collect, count, countByValue, take, top, reduce, saveAsTextFile. Word count: textFile → flatMap(split into words) → map(word → (word, 1)) → reduceByKey(+) → collect / save. DataFrames and how they are used Mark as known A DataFrame is a distributed, immutable table : rows and named columns with a schema (like a relational table). A Dataset is the typed version; DataFrame = Dataset of Row (types checked at runtime). Use: read structured data (JSON, CSV, Parquet, JDBC), then select, where / filter, groupBy, agg, join, orderBy — or register it as a view and query it with SQL (spark.sql). Why better than RDDs for structured data: because Spark knows the schema, the Catalyst optimizer can optimise the query: code → logical plan → optimised logical plan → physical plans → the cheapest by a cost model → executed as RDD operations . Same performance from every language. RDDs remain for unstructured data and low-level control. Lecture 9 8 of 8 to study Lecture 9 in full Distributed file systems I know all of this What the course says is expected Know how the different file systems work (what is on the slides). For GFS and HDFS: everything described in “The Hadoop Distributed File System: Architecture and Design”, and from “HDFS and Distributed File Systems” by Velegrakis everything mentioned on the slides. Why distributed file systems; NFS and RAID Mark as known A DFS stores files across many machines behind one namespace . Requirements: fault tolerance (with thousands of machines, failure is the norm), consistency, security, efficiency, scalability, hardware independence. NFS (Sun, 1985): a client mounts a remote directory and uses it like a local one. Stateless server; client caching and read-ahead. One server holds a file → not very fault tolerant or scalable . RAID (several disks of one machine acting as one): 0 striping (speed, no redundancy), 1 mirroring, 2–4 striping with error-correcting codes or a dedicated parity disk, 5 parity distributed over all disks (survives one disk failure). Protects against disk failure only, not machine failure. GFS: assumptions and architecture Mark as known Assumptions: commodity hardware that fails often; a modest number of huge files ; mostly large streaming reads and appends (few random writes); high sustained throughput matters more than latency. One master keeps all metadata in memory : the namespace, the file → chunk mapping, chunk locations (learned from chunkservers). Changes are recorded in a replicated operation log with checkpoints . Files are split into fixed 64 MB chunks , each with a 64-bit chunk handle , stored as ordinary files on chunkservers , 3 replicas by default. Clients ask the master only for metadata; data flows directly between clients and chunkservers — the master is never a data bottleneck. Why large chunks: fewer master interactions, less metadata, persistent connections. GFS: read, write, record append, consistency, fault tolerance Mark as known Read: client sends (file name, chunk index) → master returns the chunk handle and replica locations → client reads from the closest chunkserver. Write: the master grants one replica a lease (60 s) — the primary . The client pushes the data to all replicas , then sends the write request to the primary, which chooses a serial order and tells the secondaries to apply it in that order; they reply; the primary answers the client. On error the client retries. Record append: the client gives only the data; GFS appends it atomically, at least once , at an offset GFS chooses . If the record does not fit in the chunk, the chunk is padded and the client retries on a new chunk (a record is at most ¼ of a chunk). Replicas may contain duplicates and padding. Consistency: a region is consistent if all clients see the same data on all replicas; defined if consistent and showing exactly one mutation's write. Concurrent successful writes → consistent but undefined; failed write → inconsistent. Fault tolerance: master log replication and fast recovery, chunk version numbers to detect stale replicas, checksums (32-bit per 64 KB block), re-replication, lazy garbage collection of deleted files. HDFS: goals and architecture Mark as known Assumptions and goals: hardware failure is the norm (detect and recover automatically); streaming data access (batch, high throughput, not low latency); large data sets ; a simple coherency model: write once, read many ; "moving computation is cheaper than moving data" ; portability across hardware and software. Master/slave. One NameNode : manages the file system namespace (open, close, rename), regulates client access, and holds the block → DataNode mapping . Many DataNodes (one per node): store the blocks, serve reads and writes, and create, delete and replicate blocks on the NameNode's instruction. A file is a sequence of blocks (default 64 MB in the document; all but the last the same size). User data never flows through the NameNode. Traditional hierarchical namespace (directories and files); no hard or soft links; the replication factor is per file. HDFS: replication, rack awareness, safemode Mark as known Each block is replicated ( default factor 3 ) for fault tolerance. The NameNode makes all replication decisions and receives from every DataNode a periodic Heartbeat (it is alive) and a Blockreport (the list of its blocks). Rack-aware placement (factor 3): one replica on a node in the local rack , the second on a different node in the local rack , the third on a node in a different rack . So a block sits on two racks , never all on one rack or one node: a rack failure cannot lose it, and a write crosses racks only once (cheaper than three racks). Replica selection: a read uses the replica closest to the reader (same rack if possible). Safemode: at start-up the NameNode waits for Blockreports; a block is safely replicated when its minimum number of replicas has checked in. After a configurable percentage is safe (plus 30 s) it leaves safemode and replicates the under-replicated blocks. No replication happens during safemode. HDFS: metadata persistence (EditLog, FsImage) Mark as known EditLog: a transaction log on the NameNode's local disk recording every change to the metadata (file created, replication changed…). FsImage: a file holding the entire namespace , the file → block mapping and file-system properties. The NameNode keeps the whole image in memory . Checkpoint: at start-up it reads the FsImage, applies the EditLog, writes a new FsImage and truncates the EditLog. (The Secondary NameNode performs such checkpoints periodically; it is not a hot standby.) A DataNode stores each block as a separate local file and does not know about HDFS files; on start-up it scans them and sends the Blockreport . Communication: TCP/IP; ClientProtocol (client ↔ NameNode) and DataNode Protocol , over RPC. The NameNode only responds to requests, it never initiates them. HDFS: robustness Mark as known DataNode failure / network partition: no Heartbeat → the NameNode marks the node dead , sends it no more I/O, and re-replicates the blocks whose replica count fell below the factor. Cluster rebalancing: moving data from full DataNodes to emptier ones (planned in the document). Data integrity: the client stores a checksum for each block in a hidden file; on read it verifies and, if corrupt, fetches another replica. Metadata disk failure: FsImage and EditLog are central — the NameNode can keep multiple synchronised copies . The NameNode machine is a single point of failure ; manual intervention is needed if it fails. Snapshots: not supported in that version (planned). HDFS: data organisation, writing and deleting Mark as known Blocks: large (64 MB), because applications write once and read in streams. Staging: a client first buffers the data in a temporary local file . When a block's worth has accumulated it contacts the NameNode, which inserts the file name into the hierarchy and allocates a block and DataNodes. The client flushes the block to the first DataNode. On close, the rest is flushed and the NameNode commits the creation — a file is lost if the NameNode dies before the close. Replication pipelining: the client sends the block in small portions (4 KB) to the first DataNode , which stores each portion and forwards it to the second , which forwards to the third — a pipeline. Access: Java API, a C wrapper, the FS shell (e.g. dfs -mkdir, -cat), DFSAdmin commands, and a web browser interface. Deleting: a deleted file is moved to /trash and can be restored while it is there; after a configurable time (6 hours in the document) the NameNode removes it and the blocks are freed. Lowering the replication factor makes the NameNode pick excess replicas to delete. Lecture 10 5 of 5 to study Lecture 10 in full NoSQL I know all of this What the course says is expected From NoSQL Distilled: Chapters 1, 2, 3 and 5. Chapter 1 – Why NoSQL Mark as known Value of relational databases: persistent data, concurrency control through transactions , integration (many applications sharing one database), and a (mostly) standard model and SQL. Impedance mismatch: the relational model (flat tuples in tables) differs from in-memory data structures (nested objects), forcing translation; ORMs help but do not remove it. Integration database (shared by many applications — complex, hard to change) versus application database (owned by one application; others integrate through services ), which frees the team to choose another kind of store. Attack of the clusters: the web's data volumes need scaling out on clusters of commodity machines (cheaper and more resilient than scaling up). Relational databases are not designed for clusters . Google Bigtable and Amazon Dynamo showed the alternative. NoSQL: no strict definition. Common characteristics: not relational, run well on clusters, open source, built for 21st-century web estates, schemaless . Polyglot persistence: use different stores for different needs. Two reasons to choose NoSQL: data too big for one machine / performance, and easier development (less impedance mismatch). Chapter 2 – Aggregate data models Mark as known A data model is how we perceive and manipulate data (the storage model is how it is stored). Aggregate: a collection of related objects treated as one unit — for manipulation, for consistency / atomic updates , and for distribution on a cluster (the whole aggregate lives on one node). Example: an order with its line items, addresses and payment. The boundaries depend on how the data is accessed ; there is no single right answer. Aggregates help some queries (get the order) and hurt others (sales per product across all orders). Aggregate-oriented stores have no ACID transactions across aggregates — only atomic operations on one aggregate. Relational and graph databases are aggregate-ignorant . Model The aggregate is… Access Examples Key-value an opaque blob only by key Riak, Redis, Dynamo Document a document whose structure is visible by key, queries on fields , indexes, partial retrieval MongoDB, CouchDB Column-family a row key → column families → columns (a two-level map) by row key and column; rows may have different columns Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra Chapter 3 – More details on data models Mark as known Relationships: aggregates reference each other by id ; the database may know about the links, but updating several aggregates is not atomic . Many inter-aggregate relationships make aggregate stores awkward. Graph databases: small records with complex interconnections — nodes and edges with properties. Queries traverse edges; traversal is cheap because the work moves from query time to insert time . Usually run on one server, ACID . Opposite of aggregates. Schemaless databases: store data without defining a schema first — easy to change, handles non-uniform data. But there is always an implicit schema in the code that reads the data; the database cannot validate or optimise with it, and several applications may disagree. Materialized views: precomputed, cached results for queries that cut across aggregates; updated eagerly (with the base data) or in batch — often computed with map-reduce. Modeling for data access: design aggregates (and column families) for the queries you need; denormalise at write time. Chapter 5 – Update and read consistency Mark as known Write-write conflict: two clients update the same item at once → a lost update . Pessimistic approach: prevent it with locks (safe but can deadlock, less responsive). Optimistic: detect it — a conditional update (check that the version is unchanged) or keep both and merge . Read-write conflict (inconsistent read): a client reads in the middle of another's multi-step update → loss of logical consistency . Aggregate stores guarantee it only within one aggregate ; across aggregates there is an inconsistency window . Replication consistency: all replicas return the same value. Eventual consistency: replicas may differ for a while (stale data) but converge when updates stop. Read-your-writes / session consistency: you always see your own updates — via sticky sessions or version stamps . Chapter 5 – CAP, relaxing durability, quorums Mark as known CAP theorem: of Consistency , Availability and Partition tolerance you can have only two. A single server is CA. A cluster must tolerate partitions, so: when a partition happens, choose consistency or availability — and it is a trade-off, not binary. Often it is really consistency versus latency . Examples: hotel booking across two sites (refuse bookings, or risk a double booking); Dynamo's shopping cart is always writable and conflicting carts are merged . BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency — the counterpart of ACID. Relaxing durability: keep data in memory and flush periodically — faster, but a crash loses the latest updates (fine for session state). Replication durability fails if a node acknowledges a write and dies before replicating it. Quorums (N = replication factor): write quorum W > N/2 prevents conflicting writes; R + W > N gives strongly consistent reads. N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 is typical; W = 3, R = 1 for fast reads; W = 1 needs R = 3. Lecture 11 6 of 6 to study Lecture 11 in full Graph data management I know all of this What the course says is expected Know the Cypher query language (the features mentioned on the slides, no extra features) and the concepts on the slides. They are described in: Chapter 3 (Data Modelling) of Graph Databases for Cypher; Chapter 6 for the internals of graph databases; and, for how Neo4j achieves load balancing, the two-page Load Balancing section of Chapter 4 and the High Availability section of Seven Databases in Seven Weeks. Slide concepts: why graphs, property graph, graph DB versus analytics Mark as known Why graphs: humans think in graphs; graphs capture heterogeneous data with no fixed schema , show how parts connect, and are hard to model with relational joins . Examples: social, media, information (citation), transportation and communication networks. Property graph model: nodes (objects; can have labels ), relationships (connect two nodes; have a type and a direction ), properties (name–value pairs on nodes and relationships). Graph database versus graph analytics: a graph DB (Neo4j) is for storage and querying (like an RDBMS for tuples) — e.g. find friends of friends. Graph analytics processes the graph (k-core, centrality, PageRank) — like clustering for ordinary data. Storing graphs with relational technology means many self-joins for path queries. Neo4j: whiteboard friendly (store what you draw; values and structure only where needed), focuses on relationships, scales to tens of billions of nodes with master-slave replication. Accessed via Java, REST (JSON), Cypher , Gremlin ; Lucene -based indexing. Cypher: reading (MATCH, WHERE, RETURN) Mark as known Cypher is declarative, expressive, pattern matching — you draw the pattern in ASCII art. Node: (n) , with label (n:Person) , with property (p:Person {name: "Tom Hanks"}) (inline = exact match only). Relationship: -[:ACTED_IN]-> directed, -- / --> any type, -[r:TYPE]-> bound to r. All nodes: MATCH (n) RETURN n Filter: MATCH (m:Movie) WHERE m.released > 1990 AND m.released < 2000 RETURN m Pattern: MATCH (:Person {name:"Tom Hanks"})-[:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) RETURN m.title Order: … RETURN m.title, m.released ORDER BY m.released DESC Co-actors: MATCH (:Person {name:"Tom Hanks"})-->(:Movie)<-[:ACTED_IN]-(x:Person) RETURN x.name Chapter 3 extras: several patterns separated by commas sharing identifiers; variable-length paths -[:T 1..4]-; alternatives -[:STREET|CITY 1..2]-; anonymous node (); DISTINCT ; count(x) , collect(x) ; AS alias; a path p = (…)-[…]-(…) with length(p) ; WITH pipes one query part into the next. A query is anchored on nodes found by label + property; the rest of the pattern is matched around them. Cypher: writing (CREATE, MERGE, SET, DELETE) Mark as known Node: CREATE (p:Person {name:"Tom Hanks"}) Relationship between existing nodes: MATCH (p:Person {name:"Tom Hanks"}), (m:Movie {title:"Apollo 13"}) CREATE (p)-[:ACTED_IN]->(m) Whole pattern at once: CREATE (:Person {name:"Tom Hanks"})-[:ACTED_IN]->(:Movie {title:"Apollo 13"}) CREATE always adds (duplicates possible); MERGE creates only what is missing. SET r.rating = 97 sets a property (also on a relationship); DELETE removes — a node can be deleted only after its relationships. Other clauses named in Chapter 3: FOREACH, UNION, CREATE UNIQUE, START (deprecated). Indexes and constraints: CREATE INDEX ON :Venue(name); CREATE CONSTRAINT ON (c:Country) ASSERT c.name IS UNIQUE. Indexes find the starting nodes ; the rest is traversal. Data modelling with graphs (Chapter 3) Mark as known Relational modelling: whiteboard → E-R diagram → normalised tables with foreign keys and join tables (accidental complexity) → denormalisation for speed → slow, risky migrations . Graph modelling: the whiteboard sketch is the model; enrich it: roles → labels , attributes → properties , connections → named, directed relationships . No normalisation or denormalisation. Test the model: (1) it reads well as sentences when you follow relationships; (2) design for queryability — write the queries of your use cases. Identify elements from language: common nouns → labels , verbs with an object → relationship types , proper nouns → nodes with properties. Pitfall: do not encode an entity in a relationship . (bob)-[:EMAILED]->(charlie) loses the email; make Email a node with SENT, TO, CC, BCC. Replies and forwards are nodes too (labels Email + Reply, linked by REPLY_TO). Cross-domain models: several domains live in one graph, connected by relationships. Evolution is additive: new nodes and relationship types do not break existing queries. Graph database internals (Chapter 6) Mark as known Native graph processing = index-free adjacency: every node holds direct references to its relationships , so a hop costs O(1) . A traversal of m relationships costs O(m) instead of O(m log n) with a global index. Both directions are equally cheap; joins are effectively precomputed . Query time depends on the part of the graph visited, not its total size. Native graph storage: separate store files for nodes, relationships, labels and properties. Node and relationship records are fixed size , so a record is found at id × record size (O(1)). Node record: in-use flag, id of first relationship, id of first property, labels, flags. Relationship record: start node, end node, type, previous / next relationship for the start node and for the end node (two doubly linked lists ), first property. Properties: a singly linked list of records with key–value pairs (small values inlined, large ones in dynamic stores). Cache: an LRU-style page cache keeps hot parts of the store files in memory. APIs (high → low level): Cypher (declarative), Traversal framework , Core API (imperative), Kernel API. Transactions: Neo4j is ACID . A transaction is an in-memory object with locks on what it writes; on commit the changes go to the write-ahead log (durable once flushed), then to the store. Recovery replays the log. Scale: capacity (tens of billions of nodes/relationships), latency (traversal cost independent of size), throughput (queries touch a local subgraph). High availability and load balancing Mark as known High availability (Seven Databases): A master-slave cluster ; every instance holds the full graph . The master is elected automatically (formerly via ZooKeeper coordinators; now self-coordinating). A returning old master rejoins as a slave. Writes go to the master and are pushed to the slaves. Slaves also accept writes : the slave synchronises with the master, which propagates to the others. A write on one node is not immediately on all others → the cluster is eventually consistent (AP in CAP) and loses pure ACID. HA mainly scales reads . Weakness: it replicates the whole graph , not subgraphs — graphs cannot easily be sharded. Load balancing (Graph Databases, Chapter 4) — Neo4j has no built-in load balancer ; use the network's: Separate reads from writes: writes → the master ; reads → balanced over the whole cluster . Distinguish by HTTP method (GET vs POST/PUT/DELETE); since the REST API sends all Cypher by POST, use two load balancers (a write one and a read one) and let the application choose. Cache sharding: route requests for the same part of the graph (same user, same region) to the same instance , so that part is already in its memory cache. Works because queries are graph-local; all instances still hold all data. Read your own writes: route the write through the slave that will serve the user's next read (slower — use sparingly). Lecture 12 6 of 6 to study Lecture 12 in full Vector databases I know all of this What the course says is expected Know what vector databases are, what kind of queries they serve and what applications they may have. The slides are the guide to the concepts; know what each one is. What a vector database is and how it works Mark as known Stores multidimensional points (vectors) , not scalar values; from a few to several thousand dimensions . Purpose: swiftly and precisely locate and retrieve vectors by proximity / resemblance — semantic relevance instead of exact match (similar songs, articles, gadgets). How: traditional databases use tables, nodes or documents; vector databases use vectors and search with Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) search. Embeddings: an image, text or audio item is turned into a vector (a "code") that is a summary capturing its main points , produced by a neural network. Similar items get nearby vectors. Applications Mark as known Retail experience — recommendations from similar products and behaviour. Financial data analysis — spotting patterns and similarities in market data. Healthcare — comparing genomic data for personalised treatment. NLP applications — chatbots, virtual assistants, retrieval for language models. Media analysis — comparing images and video (medical scans, surveillance). Anomaly detection — items far from everything else (fraud, security). Challenges and features Mark as known Why they differ from relational / NoSQL systems: similarity is vague compared to exact match; similarity is more expensive to compute than exact match; vectors are large and may span many pages; vectors have no properties (attributes to sort or index on) like tuples or nodes; vectors and other forms of data must co-exist . Features of a vector database: scalability and adaptability; multi-user support and privacy; an API; a GUI. Queries they serve Mark as known Score design — how similarity is measured: basic (cosine, inner product, Euclidean, Hamming), combined (several scores merged, e.g. mean or weighted sum), learned (metric learning). Score selection = learning / choosing the best score for a task. Query types: k-NN (the k nearest vectors, exact) and ANN (approximately nearest — faster). Basic search query — (c, k)-search: find the k most similar vectors , none of which is more than c times worse than the best . No slack = exact k-NN; with slack = ANN. (A range query returns everything within a threshold.) Query variants: hybrid (similarity plus a condition on attributes, e.g. price < 100) and multi-vector (several vectors per query or item, combined with an aggregate score). Data manipulation (the embedding model): embedded in the database or as a plug-in . Indexing Mark as known Table-based: LSH (locality-sensitive hashing) — similar vectors hash to the same bucket; L2H (learning to hash) — the hash function is learned with machine learning; Quantization — map vectors to smaller vectors (compression). Tree-based: recursively partition the vectors to build a search tree. Graph-based: k-nearest-neighbour graphs (KNNG) — edges represent close similarity; monotonic search networks (MSN) and small-world graphs (SWG) — edges chosen to make the graph easy to navigate . Existing systems Mark as known Kind Example Mostly vector (native) Chroma Mostly mixed Milvus NoSQL with vectors Cassandra Relational with vectors PostgreSQL Popular: Chroma (open source), Pinecone, Weaviate (open source), Faiss (open source library), Qdrant, Milvus (open source; distributed architecture, millions of vectors, high-speed similarity search ), pgvector (an extension of PostgreSQL , for smaller scale ). Mark as read Big picture Apache Hadoop and its limits Mark difficult 1970 SQL Relational databases. ~2000 The big-data era (batch) MapReduce by Google, 2004. ~2010 The fast-data era (streaming) Apache Kafka 2011, Apache Spark 2014, Apache Flink 2015. Apache Hadoop is an ecosystem of tools for processing big data: an open-source project of the Apache group, a distributed framework written in Java. It has Google's MapReduce computation technology, HDFS (the Hadoop Distributed File System, inspired by GFS), and a framework for distributed computation in clusters — supported by Yahoo!, Facebook, Twitter, IBM and Microsoft. Technology Description MapReduce Distributed computation framework (data-processing model and execution environment) HDFS Distributed file system HBase Distributed, column-oriented database Hive Distributed data warehouse (SQL queries) Pig Higher-level data-flow language and parallel execution framework ZooKeeper Distributed coordination service Avro Data serialisation system (RPC and persistent data storage) Sqoop Bulk data transfer between structured data stores (e.g. an RDBMS) and HDFS Oozie Complex job workflow service YARN Yet Another Resource Negotiator — resource management (MapReduce v2) Flume, Mahout, Ambari Log collection, machine learning, cluster provisioning and monitoring The Apache Hadoop ecosystem. Hadoop is not a good fit for low-latency data access, lots of small files, or multiple writers with arbitrary file modifications. Its large block abstraction is what it is good at: a file can be larger than any single disk in the network, the storage subsystem is simplified (metadata bookkeeping), and replication for fault tolerance and availability is easy (Lecture 9 covers HDFS blocks and replication in detail). A job goes from HDFS to HDFS : input splits are mapped, sorted, copied and merged to reducers, and each output part is written back to HDFS with replication. Of the use cases, Hadoop handles map-only and classic MapReduce jobs well, and does not handle iterative jobs, point-to-point graph computations, streaming, or maps that communicate through shared memory. Hadoop limitation Issue with small files Slow processing speed — due to replication, I/O operations and serialisation Latency Lengthy lines of code No real-time processing No iterative processing — data must be written to disk at each iteration Security Apache Hadoop An open-source Java ecosystem for big data: MapReduce for computation, HDFS for storage. HDFS is inspired by GFS, MapReduce by Google's computation model; around them sit YARN, Hive, HBase, Pig, ZooKeeper, Sqoop, Oozie, Flume and more. Supported by Yahoo!, Facebook, Twitter, IBM and Microsoft. hadoop Hadoop limitations Small files, slow processing, latency, verbose code, no real-time and no efficient iterative processing. Slowness comes from replication, I/O and serialisation: every iteration of an algorithm is a MapReduce job that reads from and writes to HDFS. hadoop Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Spark creates an execution graph , enables in-memory computation , and needs way less code to write. How much faster? The Daytona GraySort benchmark sorts 100 TB in a distributed, parallel way. Hadoop's 2013 record: 72 minutes on 2100 machines . Spark's 2014 record: 23 minutes on 207 machines — on disk — and Spark also sorted 1 PB in 4 hours. How a Spark application runs 1 Driver program Your program runs in the driver, which holds the SparkContext — the entry point to the cluster. Reveal step 2 of 4 Installing Spark on a cluster Download and unpack a version from the Spark website, copy it to all nodes, list the worker IPs in spark/conf/slaves , put the master IP and other settings in spark/conf/spark-defaults.conf , and start everything with spark/sbin/start-all.sh . The folders: bin (shell scripts), conf , data and examples , jars (libraries), kubernetes , python , R , sbin (start/stop scripts), yarn . Apache Spark An efficient, fast, general-purpose cluster computing framework with high-level APIs in Java, Scala, Python and R. Developed from 2009 at UC Berkeley's AMPLab and open source since 2010. It builds an execution graph, computes in memory, and needs far less code than MapReduce. Spark is a processing framework, not a storage system. spark Driver, cluster manager, executors The driver program holds the SparkContext; a cluster manager assigns worker nodes; executors run tasks and cache data. The cluster manager can be Spark's standalone scheduler, YARN or Mesos. An action makes the driver turn the DAG into stages, each executed as a series of tasks on the executors. spark Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. An RDD is: immutable — operations create new RDDs, never change one; resilient and fault-tolerant — missing or damaged partitions can be recomputed after node failures; distributed — its data resides on multiple nodes; lazily evaluated — nothing is computed until it is needed; cacheable / persistent — it can be kept in memory or on disk. HTTP and FTP also give access to remote files, but as whole-file transfers, not as a file system. NFS — Sun's Network File System , around since 1985 — is the classic network file system. A client mounts a directory exported by a server into its own tree, and from then on uses it like a local directory. The server is stateless : every request (read block k of file handle h ) carries everything needed to serve it, so a server crash and restart is invisible apart from a delay. Clients cache data and read ahead to hide network latency, which means a client can briefly see stale data. NFS is simple and everywhere, but each export lives on one server: it is not very fault tolerant and not very scalable . NFS: remote files behind the same VFS interface as local ones, reached by RPC. RAID — Redundant Array of Independent Disks — works inside one machine: several disks act as one, for speed ( striping data over disks so they read in parallel) and/or reliability ( mirroring or parity ). Striping: the blocks of files A and B are spread over three disks, so they can be read in parallel. Parity levels add a parity block per stripe. Level How it works Survives RAID 0 Striping only, no redundancy — fastest No disk failure RAID 1 Mirroring: every disk has a copy One disk of each pair RAID 2 Bit-level striping with Hamming error-correcting code disks One disk RAID 3 Byte-level striping with one dedicated parity disk One disk RAID 4 Block-level striping with one dedicated parity disk — a write bottleneck One disk RAID 5 Block-level striping with the parity distributed over all disks One disk Parity: the XOR of the data blocks of a stripe, so any one lost block can be recomputed from the others. Show answer Mark as read Core concepts GFS: assumptions and design Mark difficult Google needed to store the web crawl and its derived data on thousands of cheap machines . With a server lasting about 1000 days , a cluster of 1000 servers sees about one failure per day — and copying 10 TB over a 1 Gbps network link takes about a day. The Google File System (Ghemawat, Gobioff and Leung, 2003) was designed around its workload rather than around POSIX. Assumption (GFS paper, 2.1) Consequence Component failures are the norm Constant monitoring, error detection, automatic recovery Files are huge — multi-GB is common Large blocks; few millions of files rather than billions of small ones Most files are mutated by appending, rarely overwritten Optimize appends; random writes are supported but not efficient Reads are large and streaming, or small and random High sustained bandwidth matters more than low latency Many clients append to one file concurrently Atomic record append with minimal synchronisation Co-designed with the applications A relaxed consistency model is acceptable Architecture. A GFS cluster has one master and many chunkservers , accessed by many clients . Files are divided into fixed-size chunks of 64 MB , each identified by an immutable, globally unique 64-bit chunk handle assigned by the master. Chunkservers store chunks as plain Linux files, and each chunk is replicated on three chunkservers by default (more for hot files). The master keeps all metadata: the file and chunk namespaces , the mapping from files to chunks , and the locations of each chunk's replicas . It also manages chunk leases, garbage collection and chunk migration, and talks to every chunkserver through periodic HeartBeat messages. Clients ask the master only for metadata ; all data goes directly between clients and chunkservers. No data caching : neither clients nor chunkservers cache file data — streaming reads would gain little, and the Linux buffer cache already caches chunk files on chunkservers. Clients do cache metadata . On top of the usual create, delete, open, close, read and write, GFS offers snapshot and record append . GFS architecture: control messages go to the master, data flows directly between client and chunkservers. Why a single master works A single master makes placement and replication decisions with global knowledge, which is far simpler than a distributed agreement. It does not become a bottleneck because it is never on the data path : a client asks once which chunkservers hold a chunk, caches the answer, and then reads and writes directly. Why 64 MB chunks? A large chunk size (1) cuts client–master interaction, since reads and writes on one chunk need one location lookup; (2) lets a client do many operations over one persistent TCP connection to a chunkserver; and (3) keeps the master's metadata small — less than 64 bytes per 64 MB chunk — so all of it fits in memory . The drawback: a small file of a single chunk can become a hot spot when many clients read it at once (Google saw this with an executable read by hundreds of machines, and raised its replication factor). Metadata persistence. The namespaces and the file-to-chunk mapping are made persistent in an operation log , replicated on remote machines; the master checkpoints its state (in a compact B-tree form) whenever the log grows too large, so recovery replays only the log after the last checkpoint. The chunk locations are not persisted : at start-up and in HeartBeats the master simply asks each chunkserver which chunks it has — the chunkserver has the final word anyway. GFS master The single master keeps all metadata — namespace, file-to-chunk mapping, chunk locations — in memory. Clients ask the master only for metadata and then talk to chunkservers directly, so data never flows through the master. Namespace and mapping are persisted in a replicated operation log; chunk locations are not persisted but polled from the chunkservers. gfs Chunk A fixed 64 MB piece of a GFS file, identified by a 64-bit chunk handle and stored as a Linux file on chunkservers, three replicas by default. Large chunks mean fewer master interactions, persistent TCP connections and under 64 bytes of master metadata per chunk. The drawback: a small file of one chunk can become a hot spot. gfs Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. What does the GFS master store, and where? Namespace mutations (such as creating a file) are atomic — the master handles them with locks and its operation log fixes their order. For file data, the paper defines two properties of a file region: consistent — all clients always see the same data, whichever replica they read; defined — consistent, and clients see what one mutation wrote in its entirety. Applications live with this by appending rather than overwriting , checkpointing , and writing self-validating, self-identifying records : checksums let readers skip padding and fragments, and unique record ids let them drop duplicates. Fault-tolerance mechanisms. Fast recovery — the master and chunkservers restore their state and start in seconds, however they were terminated. Chunk replication — three replicas on different machines and different racks ; the master re-replicates as soon as a replica count drops, giving priority to the chunks that lost most replicas. Master replication — the operation log and checkpoints are replicated on several machines; a mutation commits only when its log record is flushed locally and remotely. If the master dies, a new one starts elsewhere from the log. Shadow masters give read-only access while the master is down. Data integrity — each chunk is divided into 64 KB blocks , each with a 32-bit checksum , kept in memory and logged. A chunkserver verifies the checksums before returning data, so corruption never propagates; on a mismatch the reader goes to another replica and the master clones a good copy. Stale replicas — the master keeps a chunk version number and increments it whenever it grants a new lease. A replica that missed mutations while its chunkserver was down keeps an old version, is detected when the chunkserver reports its chunks, and is garbage-collected. Garbage collection. Deleting a file does not free its space immediately. The master logs the deletion and renames the file to a hidden name with the deletion timestamp. During its regular namespace scan it removes hidden files older than three days (configurable); until then the file can be undeleted by renaming it back. In the scan of the chunk namespace, the master finds orphaned chunks — not reachable from any file — and erases their metadata; in HeartBeat exchanges, chunkservers learn which of their chunks are no longer known and delete them. This lazy approach is simple and reliable in a system where creations and deletions can fail halfway. Consistent and defined regions Consistent: all clients see the same data on every replica. Defined: consistent, and showing exactly what one mutation wrote. A serial successful write leaves a region defined; concurrent successful writes leave it consistent but undefined; a failed mutation leaves it inconsistent. Record append leaves defined regions interspersed with inconsistent ones. gfs Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Consistent versus defined? Show answer Mark as read Core concepts HDFS: NameNode, DataNodes and metadata Mark difficult HDFS , the Hadoop Distributed File System , is the open-source file system modelled on GFS. It was built as infrastructure for the Apache Nutch web search engine and is part of Apache Hadoop. It is highly fault tolerant , designed for low-cost hardware , and gives high-throughput access to large data sets by relaxing a few POSIX requirements. Assumption and goal What it means Hardware failure Hundreds or thousands of machines: some component is always failing, so detection and quick automatic recovery are core Streaming data access Batch processing rather than interactive use; high throughput over low latency Large data sets Files of gigabytes to terabytes; hundreds of nodes; tens of millions of files Simple coherency model Write-once-read-many: a file once created, written and closed is not changed Moving computation is cheaper than moving data Run the computation near its data to avoid network congestion Portability Java, so it runs on heterogeneous hardware and software platforms NameNode and DataNodes. HDFS has a master/slave architecture. A cluster has a single NameNode , a master server that manages the file system namespace and regulates access by clients, and many DataNodes , usually one per machine, that manage the storage attached to their machine. A file is split into blocks stored on DataNodes. The NameNode executes namespace operations — open, close, rename files and directories — and decides the mapping of blocks to DataNodes . DataNodes serve read and write requests and create, delete and replicate blocks on the NameNode's instruction . User data never flows through the NameNode . Namespace. A traditional hierarchy: directories and files that can be created, removed, moved and renamed (Borthakur's 2007 version had no quotas, permissions or links). The NameNode records every change, including each file's replication factor — the number of copies the application asked for. HDFS architecture: metadata through the NameNode, data directly to and from DataNodes on several racks. Metadata persistence. The NameNode keeps the whole namespace and the block map in memory — compact enough that 4 GB of RAM supports a huge number of files. On disk it uses two files in its local file system: the EditLog , a transaction log recording every change to the metadata (creating a file, changing a replication factor…); the FsImage , the entire namespace including the mapping of blocks to files. At a checkpoint , the NameNode reads the FsImage and EditLog, applies all EditLog transactions to the in-memory image, writes a new FsImage and truncates the log. Several copies of both files can be kept, updated synchronously. The Secondary NameNode — a good machine, on a separate rack — takes these periodic checkpoints ( every hour ), so the EditLog does not grow without bound. It is not a standby: the NameNode is a single point of failure and its failure needed manual intervention. Later versions add high availability : an active and a standby NameNode sharing the edit logs, with ZooKeeper and failover controllers electing the leader. A DataNode knows nothing about HDFS files: it stores each block as a separate file in its local file system, spread over subdirectories. At start-up it scans its disks and sends the list of its blocks to the NameNode — the Blockreport . A checkpoint by the Secondary NameNode, every hour. High availability in later HDFS versions: an active and a standby NameNode. The NameNode executes open, close and rename, decides where blocks go and never initiates RPCs — it answers DataNodes and clients. Show answer Mark as read Interactive playground HDFS: blocks, replication and rack awareness Mark difficult Blocks. Files are shredded into blocks of a typical 64 or 128 MB (configurable per file); all blocks of a file have the same size except the last . If possible, each block of a file lives on a different DataNode. Files have strictly one writer at a time. Replication. Every block is replicated for fault tolerance — default replication factor 3 , set per file at creation and changeable later. The NameNode makes all replication decisions. It periodically receives from each DataNode a Heartbeat (the DataNode is working) and a Blockreport (the list of all its blocks). DataNode failure is the common case: with 1000 machines that last 1000 days each, expect one a day. Rack awareness. A large cluster spreads over many racks of 30–40 DataNodes; traffic between racks goes through switches, so bandwidth inside a rack is higher. Each DataNode reports its rack id to the NameNode when it registers. Replicas must not all be on the same rack, and not on the same node . Putting every replica on a unique rack survives rack failures and uses several racks' bandwidth for reads, but every write crosses racks. Borthakur's default for factor 3: one replica on a node in the local rack, another on a different node in the local rack, the last on a node in a different rack . Rack failures are far rarer than node failures, so this keeps reliability while cutting inter-rack write traffic. One third of the replicas are on one node, two thirds on one rack. Replica selection. A reader is served from the replica closest to it — same rack first, then the local data centre. Note that the storage needed is 3× the data size. Rack-aware replication and re-replication Six blocks with three replicas each over three racks. Fail DataNodes or a whole rack, then let the NameNode restore the replication factor. Click a DataNode to fail it, or fail a whole rack — no block is lost. Then let the NameNode re-replicate the under-replicated blocks from their surviving copies. Re-replication. The NameNode marks a DataNode without recent Heartbeats dead and sends it no more I/O; its blocks are no longer available, and some blocks fall below their replication factor. The NameNode constantly tracks these and starts re-replication from a surviving replica. It is also needed when a replica is corrupted, a disk fails, or a file's replication factor is increased. SafeMode. On start-up the NameNode is in SafeMode and replicates nothing. It collects Heartbeats and Blockreports; a block is safely replicated once its minimum number of replicas has checked in. When a configurable percentage of blocks is safe (plus 30 seconds), the NameNode leaves SafeMode and replicates the blocks that still have too few replicas. Rack awareness Knowing which rack each DataNode is on and placing replicas so that not all are on the same rack or the same node. Default for replication factor 3 in Borthakur's design: two replicas on two nodes of one rack and the third on a different rack. This cuts inter-rack write traffic while still surviving the loss of a whole rack. hdfs Heartbeat and Blockreport Every DataNode periodically sends a Heartbeat (I am alive) and a Blockreport (the list of all its blocks) to the NameNode.
