Reveal step 2 of 4 Reading an HDFS file. Read example: blocks A and B are read from the closest DataNodes. Staging. A create request does not reach the NameNode immediately. The client first caches the file data in a temporary local file ; when it holds more than one block, the client contacts the NameNode, which inserts the file name into the namespace, allocates a block and returns the DataNodes for it. The client flushes the block to them. On close, the rest is flushed and the NameNode commits the file creation — if the NameNode dies before the close, the file is lost. Writing remote files directly would make throughput depend on network speed and congestion. Writing a block — the replication pipeline 1 1. create() The client calls create() on DistributedFileSystem, which asks the NameNode to create the file in the namespace. Reveal step 2 of 5 Creating a file: one block written through a pipeline of three DataNodes. Writing an HDFS file: packets go down the pipeline, acknowledgements come back. Write example: block A is pipelined DN1 → DN6 → DN8. This example uses three racks; Borthakur's default policy would put two replicas on one rack. …and the acknowledgements travel back up the pipeline. Robustness. The three common failures are NameNode failures, DataNode failures and network partitions; Heartbeats and re-replication handle the DataNodes. Data integrity : when a client creates a file it computes a checksum of each block and stores them in a hidden file in the same namespace; on reading it verifies the data and fetches a block from another replica on a mismatch. Metadata disk failure is covered by keeping several synchronously updated copies of the FsImage and EditLog. Rebalancing schemes can move blocks when a DataNode runs low on space or a file is suddenly in high demand. Communication : all protocols run on TCP/IP — clients use the ClientProtocol and DataNodes the DatanodeProtocol, both wrapped in RPC . The NameNode never initiates an RPC ; it only answers. Show answer Mark as read Common mistakes Common mistakes Mark difficult Thinking data flows through the master The GFS master and the HDFS NameNode only serve metadata. Clients read and write blocks directly from and to chunkservers or DataNodes. Calling the Secondary NameNode a backup It only merges the EditLog into the FsImage every hour. It does not take over when the NameNode fails. Expecting record append to happen exactly once It is atomic and at least once : retries can leave duplicates and padding, which readers filter with checksums and record ids. Putting all replicas on different racks That is the simple policy Borthakur rejects for writes. The default places two replicas on one rack and the third on another rack. Forgetting that the last block is smaller All blocks of a file are the same size except the last one, which only holds what is left. Mark as read Summary Cheat sheet Mark difficult A DFS must be fault tolerant, consistent, secure, efficient, scalable and hardware independent — at scale, hardware failure is the norm. NFS (1985) is stateless and mounts remote directories, but is not very fault tolerant or scalable; RAID gives redundancy and speed within one machine. GFS: one master holds all metadata in memory; files are split into 64 MB chunks stored three times on chunkservers; data never flows through the master. A GFS write pushes data to all replicas, then the primary — holding a 60-second lease — orders the mutation and the secondaries apply it in the same order. Record append writes a record atomically at least once at an offset GFS chooses; if it does not fit, the chunk is padded and the client retries on a new chunk. GFS survives failures with a replicated operation log and checkpoints, 32-bit checksums per 64 KB block, chunk version numbers and lazy garbage collection. HDFS: one NameNode keeps the namespace (EditLog + FsImage) and the block map; DataNodes store blocks and send Heartbeats and Blockreports. HDFS replicates each block (default 3) rack-aware: never all on one rack or one node; writes go through a DataNode pipeline, reads use the closest replica. Mark as read Big picture Why graphs Mark difficult Humans think in graphs : we understand new things by matching them to things we know, and what we know is connected. Graphs also capture naturally heterogeneous data : there is no specific schema, they show how the different parts connect, they are hard to model with relational joins, and the connections are often what gives the most informative insights. Show answer Mark as read Core concepts The property graph model Mark difficult The property graph model has three ingredients: Nodes represent objects and can carry labels . Relationships relate two nodes, have a label used as a type , and have a direction . Properties are name–value pairs that describe characteristics, on nodes or on relationships. A small property graph: nodes A, B and C with properties, and two typed, directed relationships. Element In the example Node A name: Jo, age: 26 Node B name: Mary, age: 28 Node C name: The Mill, in: New York, builtIn: 2007 Relationship A → B type marriedTo, property in: 2005 Relationship A → C type livesIn Neo4j is called whiteboard friendly : virtually any diagram of boxes and lines on a whiteboard can be stored as it is. Compare a wine-suggestion app modelled relationally — tables categories, wines, articles and the join tables wines_categories and wines_articles — with the whiteboard version: Prancing Wolf –produced→ 2007 –grape_type→ Riesling , and Wine Expert –reported_on→ 2007 . As the saying goes, on a long enough timeline all fields become optional; a graph provides values and structure only where necessary , so there is no schema to adjust when a wine turns out to have no vintage. In Neo4j a label is not a type : two nodes labeled Wine can have completely different properties, and types must be enforced by the application if needed. The wine app as relational tables and join tables… …and the same data as drawn on a whiteboard, which is exactly how it is stored in a graph. Show answer Mark as read Core concepts RDF: graphs as triples Mark difficult RDF — the Resource Description Framework — was introduced to describe metadata on the web. Everything is a resource identified by a URI . Information is a set of statements , each a triple (subject, predicate, object) : the subject is a URI, the predicate names the relationship, and the object is another URI or a literal. For example, ( http://www.w3.org/RDF , owner, http://www.w3.org ) says W3C owns that page. Draw each statement as an edge from subject to object labeled with the predicate, and RDF data becomes a graph . Statements are resources too, so a statement can be the subject of another one — an edge can point to an edge, making it a hyper-graph . A set of triples is an RDF base . RDF Schema (RDFS) adds typing on top: rdfs:Class groups resources with a common structure; rdf:type links a resource to its classes, and every resource is an instance of rdf:Thing. rdfs:subClassOf orders classes (instances of a sub-class are instances of the super-class) and rdfs:subPropertyOf orders properties. rdfs:domain and rdfs:range restrict which classes a property may connect. RDF also has an XML syntax . Take a couple — Couple with husband John (full name John Smith) and wife Mary (Mary Wilkinson) — shown below as an RDF graph (top) and as the tree of its XML syntax (bottom). It shows the problem with storing RDF as XML: the XML tree adds rdf:RDF, Description, rdf:about and rdf:resource nodes that are not part of the RDF graph, and XML queries follow root-to-element paths while RDF queries traverse a graph. The same RDF data as a graph (top) and as the tree of its XML syntax (bottom): the XML tree has many extra nodes. First step of any relational RDF store: shorten the URIs Long URIs are fine to store but bad to index: many indexes use at most 256 or 512 characters of a key, and truncated URIs stop being unique. Stores therefore keep URIs reversed (truncation hits the common prefix), or map them to numeric identifiers — numbers also compare much faster than strings. 3Store uses hash keys for every URI and literal. Below, URIs and their identifiers are treated as the same thing. RDF Resource Description Framework: data as statements (subject, predicate, object), where subjects and predicates are URIs and objects are URIs or literals. Every statement is an edge labeled with its predicate. Statements are resources themselves, so an edge can point to an edge — the result is a hyper-graph. RDF Schema adds rdfs:Class, rdfs:subClassOf, rdfs:subPropertyOf, rdfs:domain and rdfs:range. rdf Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. What is an RDF statement? Show answer Mark as read Interactive playground Storing graphs in relational tables Mark difficult How do we store graph data using relational technologies? Building an RDF store from scratch costs effort, time and money, while relational systems have three decades of maturity, good query performance and scalability. Most RDF stores (Jena, Oracle, Sesame, 3Store, Hexastore…) therefore put a layer on top of a relational database that knows the storage scheme and translates RDF queries (SPARQL) into SQL. Check answer Show solution Mark as read Worked examples Neo4j and Cypher Mark difficult Neo4j is whiteboard friendly, focuses on the relationships between values rather than on what sets of values have in common, and scales from being embedded in an application to clusters with master-slave replication that store tens of billions of nodes and as many relationships. It ships with a web browser console (start the server with bin/neo4j start, then open the browser page on port 7474) and can be used from Java, REST, Cypher and Gremlin ; Cypher is now considered the standard. Cypher is a declarative , expressive , pattern-matching language. Nodes are written in parentheses, relationships as arrows: MATCH (n) RETURN n; // all nodes MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n; // nodes with label Person MATCH (p:Person { name : "Tom Hanks" } ) RETURN p; // inline property, exact match only MATCH (p:Person) WHERE p.name = "Tom Hanks" RETURN p; MATCH (m:Movie) WHERE m.released > 1990 AND m.released < 2000 RETURN m; // movies Tom Hanks acted in, and directed (latest first) MATCH (:Person { name : "Tom Hanks" } ) - [: ACTED_IN ] -> (m:Movie) RETURN m.title; MATCH (:Person { name : "Tom Hanks" } ) - [: DIRECTED ] -> (m:Movie) RETURN m.title, m.released ORDER BY m.released DESC ; // co-actors: any outgoing relationship to a movie, then ACTED_IN coming back in MATCH (:Person { name : "Tom Hanks" } ) --> (:Movie) <- [: ACTED_IN ] - (x:Person) RETURN x.name; Run Edit Data Cypher — a teaching interpreter, not Neo4j 💡 Try: replace "Tom Hanks" with "Meg Ryan", or change the years 1990–2000 Reading with MATCH, WHERE and RETURN on the Neo4j movie graph. CREATE (p:Person { name : "Tom Hanks" } ); MATCH (p:Person { name : "Tom Hanks" } ), (m:Movie { title : "Apollo 13" } ) CREATE (p) - [: ACTED_IN ] -> (m); CREATE (:Person { name : "Tom Hanks" } ) - [: ACTED_IN ] -> (:Movie { title : "Apollo 13" } ); // whole pattern MATCH () - [ r ] - () WHERE id (r) = 0 SET r.rating = 97 RETURN r; // property on a relationship MATCH () - [ r : short_lived_relationship ] - () DELETE r; // delete relationships first, MATCH (e:EphemeralNode) DELETE e; // then the node Run Edit Data Cypher — a teaching interpreter, not Neo4j 💡 Try: run it and read the summaries: the first CREATE adds a second Tom Hanks, so the next MATCH creates two relationships — MERGE would not Writing: CREATE, SET and DELETE. A node with relationships cannot be deleted. Paths. Friends of friends of Patty: MATCH (fof:Person)-[:friends]-(f:Person)-[:friends]-(p:Person {name: "Patty"}) RETURN fof.name. Leaving out the arrow head matches both directions. Variable-length patterns use a star: -[:ACTS_IN 1..4]- matches one to four ACTS_IN relationships. Each hop counts, so actors two degrees from Kevin Bacon are four hops away (actor–movie–actor–movie–actor). shortestPath((a)-[:ACTS_IN ]-(b)) finds the shortest connection. Use DISTINCT : without it the same actor can be counted once per path (313 instead of 304 in the book's movie data). Indexes and constraints give a schemaless graph some structure: CREATE INDEX ON :Wine(name) speeds up lookups without changing queries; CREATE CONSTRAINT ON (w:Wine) ASSERT w.name IS UNIQUE rejects duplicates, checks existing data, and creates an index automatically. On an existing database an index is populated in the background. Lookups work without an index — MATCH (v:Venue {name:'Theatre Royal'}) is correct either way — but without one Neo4j scans and filters every node with that label . Cypher, as Chapter 3 of Graph Databases presents it. Cypher describes graphs the way we draw them, as ASCII art : nodes in parentheses, relationships as --> or <-- with the type in square brackets, labels and types prefixed by a colon, properties in curly braces. Three mutual friends look like this: (emil)<-[:KNOWS]-(jim)-[:KNOWS]->(ian)-[:KNOWS]->(emil) emil, jim and ian are identifiers : they let a pattern refer to the same node twice, which is how a one-dimensional line of text describes a two-dimensional drawing. The idea is specification by example — we draw a small instance of what we are looking for. A query anchors parts of the pattern to real nodes with labels and property predicates (the bound nodes , found with the help of indexes and constraints), and Cypher then flexes the rest of the pattern around those anchors to find local matches. The anchor can be written inline or in WHERE — the two queries below are equivalent: // Jim's mutual friends: anchored inline … MATCH (a:Person { name : 'Jim' } ) - [: KNOWS ] -> (b) - [: KNOWS ] -> (c), (a) - [: KNOWS ] -> (c) RETURN b, c // … or anchored in WHERE MATCH (a:Person) - [: KNOWS ] -> (b) - [: KNOWS ] -> (c), (a) - [: KNOWS ] -> (c) WHERE a.name = 'Jim' RETURN b, c Run Edit Data Cypher — a teaching interpreter, not Neo4j A comma separates several patterns that must all match; the shared identifiers a and c tie them together. Clause What it does MATCH The specification-by-example part: the pattern to find, with anchored nodes WHERE Filters matches: paths that must be present or absent, labels or relationship types, properties that must exist or have certain values, other predicates (e.g. a date range) RETURN What to give back: nodes, relationships, properties; with DISTINCT, aggregation (count, collect), aliases (AS), ORDER BY and LIMIT CREATE / CREATE UNIQUE Create nodes and relationships (a whole pattern at once) MERGE Ensures a pattern exists: reuses the nodes and relationships that match, creates the missing ones DELETE Removes nodes, relationships and properties SET Sets property values FOREACH Performs an updating action for each element of a list UNION Merges the results of two or more queries WITH Chains query parts, piping the results of one into the next (like a Unix pipe) START Explicit starting points — deprecated in favour of anchoring in MATCH The Cypher clauses listed in Chapter 3. A Cypher statement runs in one transaction: a CREATE either adds the whole graph or nothing. CREATE versus MERGE. Use CREATE when you add to the graph and duplicates do not matter; use MERGE when the domain forbids duplication — it makes sure a subgraph is present after it runs, creating only the parts that are missing. Identifiers live only for one query ; to find a node again later, look it up by label and property (and index that combination). More pattern syntax from the Shakespeare example below: -[:STREET|CITY*1..2]- means one or two relationships, each of type STREET or CITY; () is an anonymous node you do not need later; -[w:WROTE_PLAY]- binds a relationship to the identifier w (before the colon) so WHERE or RETURN can use it; p = (…)-[…]-(…) binds a whole path , whose length(p) counts its relationships. Three domains in one graph — literary (dotted), theatrical (solid) and geospatial (dashed). Show solution Mark as read Worked examples Data modelling with graphs Mark difficult Models and goals. Modelling is an abstraction driven by a goal: there is no natural representation of the world as it really is , only purposeful selections, some more useful than others. What sets graphs apart is the close affinity between the logical and the physical model . Relational modelling forces our natural-language picture first into a logical model and then into a physical one, and each step adds semantic dissonance ; with a graph database, what we sketch on the whiteboard is what we store. Graph models and graph queries are two sides of the same coin : the model also shows which questions we want to ask. The labeled property graph, recapped: nodes hold properties (think of them as documents of key–value pairs), carry one or more labels that group them by the roles they play, and are connected by relationships that always have a direction, a single name, a start node and an end node — there are no dangling relationships. Relationships can have properties too, useful for weights, quality and constraining queries at runtime. Relational modelling of a data centre (the book's comparison) Applications run on virtual machines hosted by servers in racks behind load balancers, and use replicated databases. Operators need to find single points of failure and bill for resources. 1 Whiteboard Domain experts and architects agree on the entities and how they relate — and draw it as boxes and lines: a graph . Reveal step 2 of 5 The data centre as tables: foreign keys [FK] and join tables (AppDatabase, UserApp) are accidental complexity. Graph modelling starts the same way — a whiteboard sketch — but instead of transforming it into tables we enrich it: for every entity we capture its roles as labels , its attributes as properties and its connections as named, directed relationships . Domain modelling is isomorphic to graph modelling, so improving the domain model improves the graph model. No tables, no normalisation, no denormalisation. In the data centre graph most nodes carry two labels — a specific one (App, VM, Server) and the general Asset — so queries can target one kind of asset or all of them. The same domain as a graph: what was drawn on the whiteboard is what is stored. Testing the model. Two techniques, applied early so that later changes are driven by the business and not by poor design: Check that the graph reads well : start at a node and follow relationships, reading labels and relationship names aloud. Server 3 runs VM 31, which hosts App Instance 3 should come out as a sensible sentence. Design for queryability : write the queries the use cases need. A user reports that an application is down — which assets between the user and the application, or that it depends on, are down? MATCH (user:User) - [ *1..5 ] - (asset:Asset) WHERE user.name = 'User 3' AND asset.status = 'down' RETURN DISTINCT asset Run Edit Data Cypher — a teaching interpreter, not Neo4j 💡 Try: change *1..5 to *1..3 — which down asset is no longer reachable? Unnamed, undirected relationships of length 1 to 5 reach every asset on the paths around User 3. Nodes without a status property are excluded; DISTINCT returns each asset once however many paths reach it. Cross-domain models. A property graph joins domains without distorting them — a graph of graphs . The Shakespeare graph in the previous section connects a literary domain (Author, Play, WROTE_PLAY with a year), a theatrical one (Company, Production, Performance, Venue, User, Review) and a geospatial one (Street, City, County, Country). Relationships both partition the graph into domains and connect them; labels are first-class citizens that give each node its roles (a node can have several) and attach metadata such as indexes and uniqueness constraints. Stratford upon Avon takes part in all three domains, stored once. The business data lives in properties; the structure lives in labels and relationships, so foreign keys and cardinality constraints never pollute the data. A modelling pitfall: email provenance The goal: find suspicious email patterns, such as someone copying their own alias. 1 First attempt Users as nodes, an ALIAS_OF relationship (Alice is an alias of Bob), and the actions as relationships: (bob)-[:EMAILED]->(charlie), (bob)-[:CC]->(davina), (bob)-[:BCC]->(edward). It reads well left to right — Bob emailed Charlie . Reveal step 2 of 5 Lossy: the actions are relationships and the email is nowhere. Fixed: the email is a node with SENT, TO, CC and BCC relationships. Evolving the domain. Migrations cannot be avoided in any store, but in a graph they are usually simple: we tend to add new nodes and relationships rather than change the model in place. New relationship types do not affect existing queries — completely safe. Changing existing relationship types or the properties (not just values) of nodes may be safe, but should be checked by re-running a representative set of queries. Adding replies and forwards as relationships — (alice)-[:REPLIED_TO]->(email), (davina)-[:FORWARDED]->(email)-[:TO]->(charlie) — repeats the mistake: we cannot tell whom Alice replied to, and reusing TO mixes up recipients and forward targets. A reply is an email that is also a reply, so it becomes a node with two labels , :Email:Reply, addressed with the usual TO, CC and BCC and linked to the original by REPLY_TO. Forwards likewise become :Email:Forward nodes linked by FORWARD_OF, giving exact provenance. CREATE (reply_1:Email:Reply { id : '7' , content : 'response' } ), (reply_1) - [: REPLY_TO ] -> (email_6), (davina) - [: SENT ] -> (reply_1), (reply_1) - [: TO ] -> (bob), (reply_1) - [: TO ] -> (charlie); // who replied to email 6, at what depth (replies to replies, up to 4 deep) MATCH p = (email:Email { id : '6' } ) <- [: REPLY_TO *1..4 ] - (:Reply) <- [: SENT ] - (replier) RETURN replier.username AS replier, length (p) - 1 AS depth ORDER BY depth // how many times was email 11 forwarded? MATCH (email:Email { id : '11' } ) <- [ f : FORWARD_OF * ] - (:Forward) RETURN count (f) Run Edit Data Cypher — a teaching interpreter, not Neo4j length(p) − 1 subtracts the SENT hop, leaving the reply depth. In the book's data Davina and Bob reply at depth 1, Charlie at 2 and Bob at 3; email 11 was forwarded twice. Replies modelled in high fidelity: each reply is an Email:Reply node with a REPLY_TO link. Forwarding: a chain of Email:Forward nodes linked by FORWARD_OF. In the description of the domain… …becomes in the graph Example Common noun A label “user”, “email” → User, Email Verb that takes an object A relationship type “sent”, “wrote” → SENT, WROTE Proper noun (a person's or company's name) A node, with properties for its attributes Bob → (:User {username:'Bob'}) Identifying nodes and relationships from the language we use about the domain. Design for queryability sums up the process: Describe the client or end-user goals that motivate the model. Rewrite these goals as questions to ask of the domain. Identify the entities and relationships that appear in these questions. Translate them into Cypher path expressions . Express the questions as graph patterns , using path expressions like the ones that model the domain. Avoiding anti-patterns. Do not encode entities into relationships ; use relationships for how entities are related and the quality of that relation. Watch out for verbing — nouns turned into verbs ( to email , to google ) hide entities. Graphs are naturally additive : add new nodes and relationships freely, and do not conflate data at write time to save query time — trust the graph database to stay fast at read time. Design for queryability Model the graph from the questions you want to ask: goals → questions → entities and relationships → Cypher path expressions → graph patterns. Common nouns become labels, verbs with an object become relationship types, proper nouns become nodes with properties. Never encode an entity in a relationship: “Bob emailed Charlie” hides an Email node. modelling Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Show answer Mark as read Core concepts Inside Neo4j: native processing and storage Mark difficult Native graph processing. A graph database processes graphs natively if it has index-free adjacency : every node keeps direct references to its adjacent nodes and acts as a micro-index of its neighbourhood. A non-native engine links nodes through global indexes . Finding Alice's friends then costs an O(log n) index lookup, and finding who is friends with Alice — the opposite direction — needs one lookup per candidate, or a reverse index for every traversal direction. With index-free adjacency, relationships are physically stored, both directions are equally cheap, and bidirectional joins are effectively precomputed . Non-native processing: every hop goes through a global index. Query time depends on the part of the graph searched, not on its total size. Native graph storage. Neo4j keeps the graph in separate store files for nodes, relationships, labels and properties — the graph's structure is separate from its property data , which makes traversals fast even though the files look nothing like the user's view of the graph. Node and relationship stores use fixed-size records , so a record's position is simply id × record size : O(1) instead of an O(log n) search. Disks are slow next to memory, so Neo4j (from 2.2) uses an off-heap LRU-K page cache : each store is divided into regions, a fixed number of regions per store is cached, and pages are evicted by a least-frequently-used policy nuanced by popularity — unpopular pages leave first even if popular ones have not been touched recently. APIs form a stack, from expressive and declarative at the top to precise, imperative and bare metal at the bottom: Cypher — declarative pattern matching; tolerant to changes in the graph's structure. Traversal Framework — declarative Java: which relationship types and directions to follow, breadth- or depth-first, and an evaluator deciding at each node whether to include it and continue. Core API — imperative Java over nodes, relationships, properties and labels; lazily evaluated for reads and transactional for writes. Often the fastest, but verbose and tightly coupled to the graph's structure. Kernel API — transaction event handlers that react to transactions as they flow through the kernel, e.g. marking a node as logically deleted instead of deleting it. Neo4j's API stack. Show solution Mark as read Core concepts Transactions, availability, load balancing and scale Mark difficult Transactions. Neo4j is ACID , like a relational database. A transaction is an in-memory object holding its writes, backed by a lock manager that write-locks the nodes and relationships it touches. On commit the changes are appended to a write-ahead log ; once the commit entry is flushed to disk they are durable, are applied to the graph, and the locks are released. On rollback the object is discarded and the locks released. Concurrent changes to the same elements are serialised, with deadlock detection. From a non-shell client every query is a transaction; in the shell, :begin and :commit group statements. Recoverability. After an unclean shutdown Neo4j replays the most recent transaction log. Replaying is idempotent , so transactions already applied do no harm, and the store ends up consistent with everything committed before the failure. In a cluster a recovered instance then asks the master for newer transactions and catches up. Availability. Neo4j clusters are master-slave , with a complete replica of the graph on every machine. Writes go to the master and are replicated to the slaves at frequent intervals; some slaves may lag behind by milliseconds. The classic topology is write-master, read-slaves : writes scale only up to one machine, reads almost linearly. Neo4j also allows writing through slaves : the slave first catches up with the master, then commits synchronously on both — durable on two instances, at the cost of write latency; every write still passes through the master. Graph-local , idiomatic queries that start from a few significant nodes spread the load, use the caches well and reduce contention. HA cluster ( Seven Databases in Seven Weeks , High Availability). HA mode is Neo4j's answer to can a graph database scale? — yes, with caveats. As in MongoDB the servers elect a master that is responsible for data distribution; unlike MongoDB, slaves accept writes : a slave write synchronises with the master, which propagates it to the other slaves. A write to one slave is not immediately synchronised with all others, so for a brief moment consistency (in the CAP sense) is lost: the cluster is eventually consistent and loses pure ACID transactions across instances. In CAP terms Neo4j HA is AP , and it is presented mainly as a way to increase read capacity . Coordination used to rely on an external ZooKeeper ensemble — set unique ids for each coordinator, configure each to talk to the others and to its Neo4j server, start all three, then run each Neo4j server in HA mode with unique ports and point it at the coordinators — which meant a lot of extra administration. Newer versions are self-managing and self-coordinating : in a four-node cluster with node 4 offline, node 4 re-enters as a slave when it returns, and if master node 1 fails the others elect a new leader without any external service; the old master rejoins as a slave. To reduce the chance of reading stale data, assign a session to one server . Backups still matter for disaster recovery: neo4j-admin backup takes a full backup (a usable copy of the database) from any instance, after which incremental backups into the same directory are possible. A ZooKeeper-style coordinated HA cluster: three coordinators, one master and two slaves. Load balancing ( Graph Databases , Chapter 4). Balancing traffic over a cluster maximises throughput and reduces latency. Neo4j has no native load balancer : it relies on the load-balancing capabilities of the network infrastructure. Two techniques, plus one special case: 1. Separate read traffic from write traffic. Most writes should go to the master, so configure the load balancer to send writes to the master and balance reads across the entire cluster . In a web application the HTTP method often tells them apart: POST, PUT and DELETE may modify server-side resources, GET is side-effect free (server extensions are annotated with @GET and @POST). But the REST API submits all Cypher — reads and writes — with POST. Then use a pair of load balancers : a write load balancer that always targets the master and a read load balancer over the whole cluster, and let the application, which knows whether an operation reads or writes, pick the address. Each instance exposes a URI saying whether it is the master (and if not, which instance is), which load balancers can poll to route traffic. Separating reads and writes: writes go to the master, reads to any instance. Cache sharding: requests for the same part of the graph go to the same instance, so its cache stays warm. 2. Cache sharding. Queries are fastest when the part of the graph they need is in main memory, but a graph of billions of elements does not fit, and sharding a graph is unusually hard (see the holy grail below). Since every instance holds a full copy , route each request to the instance where the needed part of the graph is probably already cached . This works when most queries are graph-local — they start from specific nodes and traverse the surrounding subgraph — so that queries starting from the same nodes always go to the same instance. How to route consistently depends on the domain: sticky sessions , letting the instance that first served a user serve all of that user's later requests, or routing by data characteristics, e.g. requests about one geographical area to an instance warmed for it. 3. Read your own writes. Writes to the master are immediately consistent, but the cluster as a whole is eventually consistent, so the next load-balanced read may hit a slave that has not received the write yet. Fix: use the same consistent routing to send the write to the slave that will serve the subsequent read — one of the few cases where writing through a slave makes sense. Use it sparingly: writing through a slave can be an order of magnitude slower than writing to the master, so if many writes need it, throughput and latency suffer. Scale dimension What it means for Neo4j Capacity (graph size) Tens of billions of nodes, relationships and properties (34.4 billion nodes and relationships) — limited by fixed record sizes and pointers Latency (response time) An index finds the start nodes; the rest is pointer chasing, so time depends on the data queried, not on the total size Throughput (reads and writes) Locality: one business operation works on a related subgraph and does less work — e.g. latest article of an author is O(1) by following WROTE to the head of a list, older ones via PREV Constant-time reads and writes: the newest article is one WROTE hop away, older ones follow PREV. Beyond one cluster, a graph must be sharded by the application with synthetic keys, like MongoDB: traversals inside one instance stay fast, but hops between instances cost as much as a join. Mozilla's Pancake stored many small per-user graphs, which shard trivially. Automatically partitioning an arbitrary graph across machines with few cross-machine traversals is NP-hard in general — the holy grail of graph scalability. Strengths and weaknesses: open source, scales well, typeless and schemaless, Lucene lookups, Cypher and REST, constant-time traversals, HA for read-heavy sites. But HA replicates the whole graph, not subgraphs , which limits graph size; the node/relationship naming differs from vertex/edge; and the Enterprise features (HA, backups) need a commercial or AGPL licence. Neo4j high availability A master-slave cluster in which every instance holds the full graph; slaves may accept writes but synchronise through the master. Masters are elected automatically (formerly coordinated by ZooKeeper). Slaves can lag behind, so the cluster is eventually consistent — AP in CAP terms — and suited to read-heavy work. Whole graphs are replicated; subgraphs cannot be sharded. neo4j Load balancing a Neo4j cluster Neo4j has no native load balancer: send writes to the master and balance reads over the whole cluster, with two load balancers if the HTTP method cannot tell reads from writes. The REST API submits both read and write Cypher with POST, so the application chooses between a write load balancer (→ master) and a read load balancer (→ all instances). Instances expose a URI saying who the master is, which balancers poll. availability Cache sharding Route requests for the same part of the graph to the same instance, so the data they need is already in that instance's memory. Works for graph-local queries; every instance still holds the whole graph. Routing by sticky session, by user, or by domain (e.g. geography). Show solution Mark as read Common mistakes Common mistakes Mark difficult Confusing graph databases with graph analytics Neo4j stores and queries graphs; algorithms such as centrality or k-core are graph analytics on top of the data. Treating labels as types Nodes with the same label can have completely different properties. Neo4j enforces nothing unless you add constraints. Counting degrees as hops In an actor–movie graph one degree between actors is two ACTS_IN hops: two degrees need *1..4. Forgetting DISTINCT The same node can be reached along several paths; count(DISTINCT x) avoids counting it more than once. Putting multi-valued properties in a property table First normal form allows one value per column; multi-valued properties such as author go to the excess table. Calling Neo4j HA strongly consistent One instance is ACID, but a cluster's slaves may lag: HA is eventually consistent (AP) and aimed at reads. Hiding an entity in a relationship (bob)-[:EMAILED]->(charlie) loses the email itself. When a verb hides a noun (email, order, review, payment), make the noun a node. Using CREATE where MERGE is needed CREATE always adds, so a repeated import creates duplicates. MERGE reuses what is already there. Expecting Neo4j to balance load itself There is no native load balancer: the network's balancers route writes to the master and reads to the cluster. Thinking cache sharding partitions the graph Every instance still stores the whole graph; cache sharding only routes requests so that each instance's cache holds a different part of it. Mark as read Summary Cheat sheet Mark difficult Graphs capture heterogeneous data with no fixed schema and show how the parts connect — hard to model with relational joins. Property graph: nodes with labels, directed relationships with a type, and name–value properties on both. RDF stores everything as (subject, predicate, object) triples of URIs and literals; RDFS adds classes, sub-classes, sub-properties, domains and ranges. Vertical table: one triple table, great for heterogeneous data and single-triple queries, but path and multi-property queries need many self-joins. Property tables remove joins for common single-valued properties (rest in an excess table); vertical partitioning keeps one two-column table per predicate; hexastores index all six orders of s, p, o. Cypher is declarative pattern matching: MATCH (a)-[:TYPE]->(b) WHERE … RETURN …; CREATE adds, MERGE adds only what is missing, WITH chains query parts; Gremlin is a step-by-step traversal (pipes) language. Graph modelling has no tables, normalisation or denormalisation: common nouns become labels, verbs become relationships, things become nodes — and an entity hidden in a verb ("emailed") must become a node (Email). Index-free adjacency: each node points directly to its relationships, so a hop costs O(1) instead of an O(log n) index lookup — traversals cost O(m), not O(m log n). Neo4j is ACID with a write-ahead log; HA is master-slave with full-graph replicas and eventual consistency across slaves (AP); graphs cannot be auto-sharded. Neo4j has no built-in load balancer: send writes to the master and reads to the whole cluster, route requests for the same part of the graph to the same instance (cache sharding), and write through a slave only to read your own writes. Show answer Mark as read Core concepts Data models, database types and ACID Mark difficult Every database is built on a data model , which has three components: Structures — how data is organised (relations, documents, key-value pairs, graphs…). Constraints — the rules data must satisfy (keys, foreign keys, domains…). Operations — what you can do with it (relational algebra and SQL, document queries, graph traversals…). Different families of databases make different choices for each component. Type Stores data as Examples Relational Tables with predefined schemas and relationships between them Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server Document Documents, often in JSON or BSON format MongoDB, CouchDB Key-value Key-value pairs for fast retrieval Redis Columnar Columns instead of rows, for analytical queries Cassandra, HBase Graph Graphs, managing entities and their relationships Neo4j Time series Timestamped or time-series data, optimised for it InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Prometheus Object-oriented Objects, as used in object-oriented programming ObjectStore In-memory Data kept primarily in memory for fast retrieval DuckDB, Memcached Vector High-dimensional vectors, stored, indexed and searched efficiently Pinecone, Milvus Nine database types you must know. Relational databases bring structured data, SQL, transactions with ACID, indexing and optimisation; NoSQL systems add distributed architectures and new data models, and NewSQL tries to combine both. Relational systems guarantee ACID transactions: Property Meaning Atomic Each transaction is either properly carried out, or the process halts and the database reverts to the state before the transaction started — so all data in the database is valid. Consistent A processed transaction will never endanger the structural integrity of the database. Isolated Transactions cannot compromise the integrity of other transactions by interacting with them while they are still in progress. Durable The data of a completed transaction persists even through network or power outages; a failed transaction does not affect the data. “No indexes, please — I'm allergic to them” A well-known comic sums up the background: a query with one SELECT on a very big table, eight joins, five subqueries and a GROUP BY, sent to MySQL without indexes — and its author is still waiting at the counter long after everyone else. The rest of this lecture is about the indexes that would have saved them. Data model Three components: structures, constraints and operations. In the relational model the structures are relations, the constraints are keys, foreign keys and domains, and the operations are relational algebra and SQL. Every database family — relational, document, key-value, columnar, graph, time-series, object-oriented, in-memory, vector — makes a different choice for each of the three. background ACID Atomic, consistent, isolated, durable — the guarantees of a transaction. Atomic : the transaction is carried out completely or the database reverts to the state before it started. Consistent : a processed transaction never endangers the structural integrity of the database. Isolated : transactions cannot compromise each other while still in progress. Durable : the effects of a completed transaction persist through network or power outages. background Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. A hash function h h h takes a hash-key value and produces a bucket number , an integer from 0 0 0 to B − 1 B - 1 B − 1 . The defining intuition is that h h h randomises hash-keys: if keys are drawn from a reasonable population, h h h sends roughly equal numbers of them to each of the B B B buckets. (A population smaller than B B B is not reasonable — some buckets must stay empty.) For integer keys the common choice is h ( x ) = x m o d B h(x) = x \bmod B h ( x ) = x mod B . It works well when the population is all positive integers — each bucket gets 1 / B 1/B 1/ B of them. With B = 11 B = 11 B = 11 each bucket receives 1 / 11 1/11 1/11 of the even integers. In general, a B B B sharing a factor with all (or most) keys gives a skewed distribution, so choose B B B prime — though you still have to watch for keys that are all multiples of B B B itself. Show solution Mark as read Big picture Disks, blocks and why indexes exist Mark difficult An index is a data structure that makes it efficient to retrieve objects given the value of one or more of their fields — the search key . Given a value v v v , the index returns the records with v v v in that field without reading the whole file. A hash table is the simplest way to build one: hash the phone field of every (name, address, phone) record, put each record in its bucket (a linked list in memory, or a disk block), and later hash a phone number to find the only bucket worth searching. With roughly as many buckets as records, each bucket holds only a few. Why do indexes matter so much for large data? Because of secondary storage . Disks are organised into blocks , the minimum unit moved between disk and memory (64 KB in the book's example). Accessing and reading a block takes about 10 ms — at least five orders of magnitude ( 10 5 10^5 1 0 5 ) slower than reading a word from main memory. If you only need a few bytes, having them in memory is overwhelmingly better; if you process every byte of a block, moving the block still costs far more than the computation. Placing related data on one cylinder (the blocks reachable without moving the disk head) reads them much faster than 10 ms per block, but a disk cannot transfer more than about 100 MB per second however the data is laid out. A megabyte is no problem; a hundred gigabytes or a terabyte is a problem just to read . So cost is counted in page I/Os In the rest of the course, and in the database textbook, the cost of an index operation is the number of disk pages it reads or writes. The CPU work in between is negligible by comparison. The textbook motivates tree indexes the same way. A file sorted on g p a gpa g p a can answer gpa > 3.0 by binary search, but binary search on a large file still fetches many pages. Build a second, much smaller file with one entry per data page — (first key on page, pointer to page) — and binary-search that instead. Repeat the construction on the index file until the top fits on one page, and you have a tree. Alternative Data entry k* is… Consequence (1) the data record itself, with key value k The index is the file organisation itself; it is necessarily clustered. (2) ⟨k, rid⟩ — the id of a record with key k Small entries; the records live in a separate data file. (3) ⟨k, list of rids⟩ — all records with key k Most compact for duplicates; entries vary in length. What an index stores for each search key value. Upper tree levels hold index entries ⟨key, page pointer⟩ that only direct the search. An index is clustered when the data records are stored in the same order as its data entries — or close to it — and unclustered otherwise. Suppose alternative (2) is used and the records sit in a heap file. To build a clustered index, first sort the heap file, leaving some free space on each page for future inserts. Overflow pages may still be needed later, so the order of the records is close to , but not identical to, the sort order. A file can be clustered on at most one search key. Why clustering matters Both indexes lead you to the right data entries in sorted order. With a clustered index the matching records are packed on consecutive pages, so a range query reads one page per page of results. With an unclustered index consecutive data entries point all over the data file, so a range query can cost one I/O per record . Index A data structure that retrieves the objects with a given value in one or more fields without scanning all of them. A hash table on the phone field of (name, address, phone) records is the simplest example: hash the phone, go to that bucket, and search only it. The fields the index is built on form its search key . MMDS 1.3.3 indexing Data entry k* What an index stores for search key value k: the record itself, ⟨k, rid⟩, or ⟨k, list of rids⟩. Show answer Mark as read Interactive playground Hash indexes: static, extendible, linear Mark difficult Hash-based indexes are excellent for equality selections and useless for range selections: hashing deliberately scatters neighbouring values. The textbook builds up three schemes. Static hashing. The file is a fixed collection of N N N buckets, numbered 0 0 0 to N − 1 N - 1 N − 1 . Each bucket has one primary page and possibly a chain of overflow pages . To search, insert or delete k ∗ k* k ∗ , compute h ( k ) m o d N h(k) \bmod N h ( k ) mod N and work in that bucket only; an entry that does not fit goes to a new overflow page. Searching ideally costs one I/O, insert and delete two (read and write the page). The problem is that N N N is fixed. If the file shrinks, space is wasted; if it grows, long overflow chains develop and every search must walk them. Keeping pages 80% full at creation delays the problem, and periodically rehashing into more buckets cures it — but rehashing takes time and the index is unusable meanwhile. Static hashing shares this drawback, and its concurrency advantage, with the static tree index ISAM. Extendible hashing fixes this with one idea: keep a directory of pointers to buckets, and double the number of buckets by doubling only the directory , splitting only the bucket that overflowed. The hash value is read as a binary number and its last d d d bits index the directory, where d d d is the global depth . Each bucket also has a local depth l l l : all its entries agree on their last l l l bits. Extendible hashing, step by step The textbook's file: global depth 2, four buckets of four entries. Insert keys and watch which ones fit, which split a bucket, and which double the directory. The textbook first presents ISAM , a static tree: the leaf pages are allocated sequentially when the file is created, inserts that do not fit go to overflow pages, and only leaf pages are ever modified, so the index levels never need locking. It works well for data that rarely changes; with many inserts to the same leaf, long overflow chains form. The B+ tree is the dynamic structure that adjusts gracefully to inserts and deletes and is the most widely used index of all. Its shape in two lines: Leaf pages contain data entries and are chained (previous and next). The MapReduce programming model Input and output are each a set of key/value pairs . The programmer specifies two functions: map(in_key, in_value) -> list(out_key, intermediate_value) processes an input pair and produces a set of intermediate pairs; reduce(out_key, list(intermediate_value)) -> list(out_value) combines all intermediate values for one key and produces a set of merged output values (usually just one). In between, the system groups by key . The model is inspired by primitives from functional languages such as Lisp, Scheme and Haskell. def map (input_key, input_value): # input_key: document name, input_value: document contents for word in input_value.split(): emit_intermediate(word, 1 ) def reduce (output_key, intermediate_values): # output_key: a word, intermediate_values: a list of counts result = 0 for v in intermediate_values: result += v emit(output_key, result) “What does this do?” — Google's classic example: word count. Check answer Show solution Mark as read Visual explanation How a MapReduce job runs Mark difficult Implementation There is one master node. The master partitions the input file into M splits, by key. The master assigns workers (= servers) to the M map tasks and keeps track of their progress. Workers write their output to local disk, partitioned into R regions. The master assigns workers to the R reduce tasks. Reduce workers read their regions from the map workers' local disks. Map task Split → record reader → map → combine Reads its split from HDFS, parses records, applies map and the optional combiner, and writes partitioned output to local storage . Reduce task Copy → sort → reduce Copies its region from every map worker, sorts and merges by key, applies reduce, and writes the result as a file to HDFS . Hadoop at a glance : data on HDFS is divided into input partitions, one map per partition, the map outputs are shuffled across the network, sorted in parallel, reduced, and written back to HDFS as output partitions. Failures (MMDS §2.2.6) are the normal case when thousands of components run for hours. The master pings workers periodically. If a map worker fails, all its map tasks are redone — even completed ones, because their output sat on that node's local disk — and the reduce tasks are told where to read instead. If a reduce worker fails, its running tasks are simply rescheduled. Only the failure of the master forces the whole job to restart. Where MapReduce runs. Cluster computing uses a large number of commodity servers connected by a high-speed commodity network: a rack holds a small number of servers (8–64 in the book), a data center holds many racks, and racks are connected by a switch. In the design space of systems — transaction processing, shared-memory and data-parallel search, HPC, grid — this is DISC , data-intensive scalable computing. Of the parallel architectures (shared memory, shared disk, shared nothing), shared nothing scales to thousands of computers; shared memory is easiest to program, but expensive. It relies on a distributed file system (MMDS §2.1): huge files, rarely updated, divided into chunks of typically 64 MB, each replicated (perhaps three times) on different racks, with a master node recording where the chunks are. Lecture 9 covers GFS and HDFS in detail. Master and workers The master creates M map and R reduce tasks, assigns them to workers, and tracks their status. Usually one map task per input chunk (split). Map workers write their output to local disk, partitioned into R regions; the master tells reduce workers where to read them. Mark as read Big picture Why databases, and why relational Mark difficult Why would we want a database at all? It solves four problems: Sharing — concurrent access by multiple readers and writers. Data model enforcement — all applications see clean, organized data. Scale — work with data sets too large to fit in memory. Flexibility — use the data in new, unanticipated ways. A data model has three components: structures , constraints and operations . A raw genome annotation file has none of them — a stream of lines whose meaning lives only in the program that reads it. The relational model (Codd, 1970): everything is a table, every row of a table has the same columns, and relationships are implicit — a student id in one table matches a student id in another, with no pointers. In the book's terms a tuple is a set of name–value pairs, a relation a set of tuples, and SQL operations consume and return relations. Value of relational databases (NoSQL Distilled 1.1) What it means Getting at persistent data Keep large amounts of data on a backing store, with more flexible access than a file Concurrency Many users and applications at once; transactions handle errors and conflicting updates Integration Several applications share one database and see each other's data A (mostly) standard model The same relational model, SQL and transactions across vendors Data model versus storage model The data model is how we perceive and manipulate data (Lecture 1); the storage model is how the database stores it internally. Distinct from the storage model, which describes how the database stores the data internally. NoSQL Distilled uses “data model” for the way the database organizes data — more formally a metamodel. models Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Show answer Mark as read Core concepts Impedance mismatch Mark difficult Application developers' biggest frustration with relational databases is the impedance mismatch : the difference between the relational model and the in-memory data structures of the program. Relational tuples must hold simple values — no nested records, no lists. An order on screen is one structure: an id, a customer, a list of line items, and payment details. In the database it is split into rows of orders , customers , order lines and credit cards , and has to be translated back and forth on every save and load. Impedance mismatch: one order in memory becomes rows in four tables. Why object databases did not win In the 1990s many expected object-oriented databases — which store in-memory structures directly — to replace relational ones. They faded: relational databases won through their role as an integration mechanism with a mostly standard language (SQL). Object-relational mappers such as Hibernate and iBATIS remove a lot of the grunt work, but the mapping problem remains, and ignoring the database leads to poor query performance. Relational tuples hold only simple values — no nested records or lists — so an order with line items and payment details is split over several tables. Object-relational mappers such as Hibernate reduce the work but not the problem. motivation Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Why does an order cause an impedance mismatch? An organization has many sources of data. Two classic architectures bring them together: A data warehouse : data cleaning and ETL tools (extract–transform–load) copy the sources into one relational warehouse, used for OLAP, decision support, data cubes and data mining. Virtual integration : data stays in the sources (relational databases, Excel files, web sites, web services), each with a local schema; users query a global schema , and schema mappings translate the queries to the sources. Data warehouse architecture. Virtual integration architecture: the data stays in the sources. Within applications, the book contrasts two roles for a database: An integration database is shared by several applications, usually built by separate teams. Everybody sees a consistent set of data, but the schema becomes far more complex than any one application needs, every change needs coordination, an index that helps one application can hurt another's inserts, and the database must enforce integrity itself because it cannot trust the applications. An application database is accessed only by a single application codebase owned by one team. The team evolves the schema and keeps integrity in its own code. Other applications integrate through services — web services exchanging richer structures (XML or JSON documents with nested records and lists) over HTTP. Once the database is hidden behind services, the outside world no longer cares how the data is stored — so the team is free to use a non-relational store. The speculative retailer's web application below is an example: user sessions, financial data, shopping cart, recommendations, product catalog, reporting, analytics and activity logs could each use a different store. Polyglot persistence: each part of the application can use the store that suits it. Integration vs application database An integration database is shared by several applications; an application database is accessed by one application owned by one team. Integration databases become complex and every change needs coordination. Application databases let the team evolve the schema, enforce integrity in code, integrate through services (XML or JSON over HTTP), and choose a non-relational store. motivation Polyglot persistence Using different data stores for different circumstances within one organization or application. Show answer Mark as read Big picture Clusters and the birth of NoSQL Mark difficult The need for scaling up. Data used to be produced by employees; then came internet users, and now machine-generated data — far more again. Websites track activity in detail and serve huge numbers of visitors: lots of traffic . There are two ways to cope: Scale up : a bigger machine with more processors, disk and memory. It gets ever more expensive and has real limits. Scale out : a cluster of many small commodity machines. Cheaper at this scale, and more resilient: individual machines fail, but the cluster keeps going. SQL is happy on one big server and unhappy on the cluster. Relational databases are not designed for clusters : clustered relational databases (Oracle RAC, SQL Server) share a disk subsystem, which remains a single point of failure; running separate servers for different data ( sharding ) leaves the application to track which server holds what, and loses querying, referential integrity, transactions and consistency across shards. Licences priced per server made it worse. late 1990s Strozzi NoSQL An open-source relational database that did not use SQL — unrelated to today's meaning. 2000s Bigtable and Dynamo Google and Amazon, running huge clusters, publish papers on Bigtable and Dynamo . 11 June 2009 The NoSQL meetup Johan Oskarsson organizes a San Francisco meetup on open-source, distributed, non-relational databases; “NoSQL” is chosen as a Twitter hashtag. Talks: Voldemort, Cassandra, Dynomite, HBase, Hypertable, CouchDB, MongoDB. There is no definition of NoSQL — only common characteristics: non-relational , cluster-friendly , open source , built for the 21st-century web , and schema-less . (“Not Only SQL” does not really work: Oracle would qualify.) The book's reading: an ill-defined set of mostly open-source databases, mostly developed in the early 21st century, mostly not using SQL. NoSQL is best seen as a movement whose main result is polyglot persistence : relational databases remain one option — and still the most common — among several. There are two reasons to consider NoSQL: large-scale data that demands a cluster, and easier development through a more convenient data interaction style. Scaling up vs scaling out Up: a bigger machine. Out: many small commodity machines in a cluster — cheaper at scale and more resilient. Relational databases are not designed for clusters: shared-disk clusters keep a single point of failure, and application-level sharding loses cross-shard queries, integrity and transactions. motivation NoSQL An ill-defined set of mostly open-source, mostly 21st-century databases that mostly do not use SQL. Show answer Mark as read Core concepts Aggregates Mark difficult The relational model splits data into tuples , which cannot nest. Aggregate orientation recognizes that we often want to operate on a more complex unit — a record with nested lists and records. The term comes from Domain-Driven Design: an aggregate is a collection of related objects that we wish to treat as a unit for data manipulation and consistency. We update aggregates atomically and communicate with the store in terms of aggregates. The order from the impedance-mismatch figure is exactly that: stored as one Order 1001 aggregate instead of rows in four tables. In UML the order contains its line items (the black diamond, composition). The whole order stored as one aggregate. // in customers { "id" : 1 , "name" : "Martin" , "billingAddress" : [{ "city" : "Chicago" }] } // in orders { "id" : 99 , "customerId" : 1 , "orderItems" : [ { "productId" : 27 , "price" : 32.45 , "productName" : "NoSQL Distilled" } ], "shippingAddress" : [{ "city" : "Chicago" }], "orderPayment" : [ { "ccinfo" : "1000-1000-1000-1000" , "txnId" : "abelif879rft" , "billingAddress" : { "city" : "Chicago" } } ] } Two aggregates: customer and order (NoSQL Distilled, 2.1.1). Notice three choices: The address appears three times , copied as a value rather than referenced by id — we do not want an order's shipping address to change when the customer moves. The product name is denormalized into the order item, so reading an order touches fewer aggregates. The link from order to customer ( customerId ) is a relationship between aggregates. The boundary could also be drawn differently: put all orders inside the customer aggregate. Which is right depends entirely on how the data is accessed — the customer with all orders at once, or one order at a time. Consequences of aggregate orientation. Aggregate-ignorant models — relational and graph — do not know about aggregates. That is not bad: if the same data is used in many contexts, there may be no good boundary. Orders make good aggregates for customers and order processing, but to analyze product sales over months you would have to dig into every order (a product / revenue / prior revenue report like the one below). Clusters : an aggregate tells the database which data is used together and should live on the same node — the clinching reason for aggregates. Transactions : aggregate-oriented databases support atomic updates of a single aggregate , not ACID transactions across aggregates; atomicity across aggregates must be handled in the application. Graph and other aggregate-ignorant databases usually support ACID. A product sales report: this cuts across every order aggregate. Aggregate A collection of related objects treated as a unit for data manipulation and consistency (from Domain-Driven Design). Aggregates are the unit of atomic updates and the natural unit for sharding and replication. Show solution Mark as read Worked examples Key-value, document and column-family Mark difficult Four families of NoSQL databases: key-value (Redis, Riak, Project Voldemort), document (MongoDB, CouchDB, RavenDB), column-family (Cassandra, HBase) and graph (Neo4j). The first three are aggregate-oriented . Key-value and document stores both hold many aggregates, each under a key. In a key-value store the value — the aggregate — is opaque : a blob the database does not look into. You can store anything (up to a size limit), but you can only look it up by key and get the whole aggregate. In a document store the database sees the structure of the aggregate. It limits what you can store, but you can query on fields , retrieve part of a document, and index its contents. There is no schema: the next order document may carry a field such as "discount-code" that the others lack. The line is blurry: key-value stores add metadata (Riak can attach customer_id:7231 to a value for indexing and links; Redis splits values into lists and sets), and document stores use an id field for key-style lookups. Still, value == aggregate and document == aggregate. Documents have no schema: the second order carries a field the first does not. Column-family stores follow Google's Bigtable (HBase, Cassandra). Think of a two-level map : a row key (1234) selects the aggregate, and inside it column families group columns (column key → column value) that are usually accessed together. Customer 1234 in a column-family store. Row key Column family Column key Column value 1234 profile name "martin" 1234 profile billingAddress data… 1234 profile payment data… 1234 orders OR1001 data… 1234 orders OR1002 data… 1234 orders OR1003 data… Customer 1234 in a column-family store: get('1234', 'name') returns "martin". Two ways to read it: row-oriented — each row is an aggregate, with column families as useful chunks of it; column-oriented — each column family is a record type, and a row is the join of its records across families. Skinny rows have few columns shared by all rows (a record); wide rows have many different columns (a list, e.g. one column per order). Columns can be sorted , so keys like 20111027-1001 give date ranges. New columns are added freely; new column families rarely. Cassandra calls the inner level super columns . Model Aggregate is Access Key-value Opaque value Lookup of the whole aggregate by key Document Transparent document, no schema Queries on fields, partial retrieval, indexes Column-family Row divided into column families Row key plus column; families as units of access Graph No aggregates — nodes and edges Traversal along relationships Summary of the data models (NoSQL Distilled 2.4). Key-value and document stores Both store aggregates under a key. Key-value: the aggregate is opaque. Document: the database sees its structure. A key-value store allows only lookup by key of the whole aggregate. A document store allows queries on fields, partial retrieval and indexes on the contents. In practice the line is blurry (Riak metadata, Redis lists and sets). aggregates Column-family store A two-level map: a row key selects an aggregate, which is divided into column families of columns (Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra). Column families group data that is accessed together. Skinny rows have few, shared columns (a record); wide rows have many different columns (a list), which can be sorted, e.g. by date-id keys. aggregates Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Data that is related is not always accessed together — orders may need to be processed on their own, yet look up their customer. The simplest link is to embed the customer id in the order and make a second call. Many stores let the database know about such links (indexes in document stores, link metadata in Riak). But atomicity covers one aggregate : updating several at once means handling a failure halfway yourself. Aggregate-oriented databases grow awkward as you work across aggregates — yet relational databases are no stars at complex relationships either: SQL with many joins becomes hairy and slow. Graph databases take the opposite approach to aggregates: small records with complex interconnections — nodes connected by edges, with properties. Queries such as find the books in the Databases category written by someone whom a friend of mine likes follow the edges. Traversal is cheap because the work of navigating relationships is moved from query time to insert time . They suit social networks, product preferences and eligibility rules, usually run on a single server, and support ACID transactions across nodes and edges. Examples: Neo4j, Sparksee, OrientDB, GraphDB, AllegroGraph, Blazegraph, RDF stores. Lecture 11 covers graph databases in depth. Schemaless databases. All NoSQL families let you store data without defining a schema first: any value under a key, any document, any column, any new edge or property. That makes it easy to change what you store as you learn, and to handle nonuniform data without sparse tables or meaningless columns like customField6 . But there is nearly always an implicit schema . Code such as anOrder["price"] * anOrder["quantity"] assumes those fields exist and hold numbers; a program cannot guess that qty means quantity . So: to understand the data you must read the application code; the database cannot use the schema to store data efficiently or validate it; several applications sharing the store can disagree — mitigated by encapsulating the store in one application (services again) or giving each application its own section of the aggregate; the flexibility applies within an aggregate — changing aggregate boundaries is as hard as any relational migration. Materialized views. Aggregates work against queries that cut across them — how much did this product sell in the last two weeks? Relational databases answer with views , computed on access, and materialized views , computed in advance and cached on disk, for data read often that may be slightly stale. NoSQL stores reuse the term for precomputed, cached queries, often built with map-reduce . Two strategies: Eager : update the view together with the base data (adding an order also updates each product's purchase history) — good when reads of the view outnumber writes and freshness matters. Batch : recompute at regular intervals — cheaper writes, staler views. Views can live outside the store, be computed by the store, or sit inside an aggregate (an order summary in the order document) or in their own column family , updated in the same atomic operation. Modeling for data access. Design aggregates for the reads you need: Key-value, everything embedded : one key returns the customer with all orders, but to list orders or products the client reads and parses the whole value. Splitting into Customer and Order objects with references (the customer keeps a list of order ids) lets orders be found independently, at the cost of updating the customer on every new order. Analytics aggregates : on each order, update an item aggregate such as {"itemid": 27, "orders": [99, 545, 897, 678]} — real-time BI instead of end-of-day batch runs. Document store : since you can query inside documents, the customer no longer needs a list of order ids; find orders by customerId. Column-family : model for the queries , not for writing — denormalize during the write; order columns so frequent ones are fetched first. Graph : customers, orders and products are nodes connected by typed, directed relationships such as PURCHASED, PAID_WITH and BELONGS_TO. Graph database Small records (nodes) with complex interconnections (edges); traversals are cheap because work moves from query time to insert time. Good for social networks, product preferences and eligibility rules. Graph databases usually run on one server and support ACID transactions across nodes and edges. Built eagerly on every update of the base data, or in batch jobs at intervals; often computed with map-reduce. Can live inside an aggregate or in its own column family. models Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Why are traversals cheap in a graph database? Show answer Mark as read Core concepts Update and read consistency Mark difficult ACID (atomic, consistent, isolated, durable — defined in Lecture 1) is the relational answer. The book's point: its real core is atomicity across many rows and tables , and consistency in a cluster is much more involved than ACID or not . This section looks at the kinds of inconsistency a NoSQL store has to deal with. Update consistency. Martin and Pramod update the same phone number at the same time — a write-write conflict . The server serializes the writes; without concurrency control, Martin's is applied and immediately overwritten: a lost update , because Pramod's write was based on the state before Martin's. Pessimistic approaches prevent conflicts, typically with write locks : only Martin gets the lock, and Pramod sees his result first. Risk: poor responsiveness and deadlocks — a trade-off between safety and liveness . Optimistic approaches detect conflicts: a conditional update tests that the value is unchanged since it was read, so Pramod's update fails and he must look again. Or save both updates, mark the conflict and merge — as in version control, often with domain-specific logic. With several servers, they must also agree on the order of updates — sequential consistency . Replication makes write-write conflicts more likely unless one node handles all writes for a piece of data. Nick and Mary: the business transaction problem 1 Both read Nick and Mary each GET the same record through their browsers and servers; both see version v101 . Reveal step 2 of 4 Offline lock with a version stamp. Read consistency. Martin adds a line item and then updates the shipping charge; Pramod reads in between and sees new items with the old charge — a read-write conflict (an inconsistent read), breaking logical consistency . Relational databases prevent it with transactions. Aggregate-oriented stores give it within one aggregate — so put the line items and shipping charge in the order aggregate. Across aggregates, there is an inconsistency window (Amazon SimpleDB: usually under a second). Replication adds replication consistency : the same item read from different replicas should have the same value. Pramod in Mumbai books the last hotel room; the update reaches Boston before London, so Cindy sees it booked while Martin sees it free. The system is eventually consistent : if updates stop, all replicas converge. Out-of-date data is stale . Consistency can often be chosen per request . Worst is inconsistency with yourself: you post a comment, refresh, hit another node and your comment is gone. Read-your-writes consistency (one of the session guarantees of Lecture 3) — usually provided as session consistency — fixes this, with sticky sessions (session affinity to one node) or version stamps that every node checks before answering. Write-write and read-write conflicts Write-write: two clients update the same item at once (lost update). Read-write: a client reads in the middle of another client's write. Pessimistic approaches prevent conflicts with locks; optimistic approaches detect them, e.g. with conditional updates or by saving both versions and merging. consistency Replication and eventual consistency Replicas may disagree for a while, but if updates stop, they all eventually converge to the same value. The time a read can see inconsistent data is the inconsistency window. Read-your-writes (session) consistency guarantees that you see your own updates, using sticky sessions or version stamps. consistency Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Show answer Mark as read Core concepts Relaxing consistency: CAP and BASE Mark difficult The CAP theorem — consistency, availability, partition tolerance; under a partition, choose C or A — is defined in Lecture 3 ( CAP, PACELC and consistency ). This section adds the NoSQL Distilled view of it. The effect of replication. Nick and Mary write to one database: no problem. Replicate it, and the link between the replicas can break — a split brain . Then either the system refuses the writes until it can coordinate — consistency guaranteed — or it accepts both on their own sides — availability guaranteed , at the cost of divergence. A single server is CA because it cannot partition; a cluster must tolerate partitions, and the choice is not binary : you can trade a little consistency for some availability. Partition, option 1: refuse writes — consistency guaranteed. Partition, option 2: accept writes on both sides — availability guaranteed, the replicas may diverge. Side of the triangle Systems (after S. Tiwari) C + P Bigtable, HBase, Hypertable A + P Dynamo, Riak, Voldemort, Cassandra, CouchDB C + A RDBMS Where systems sit in the CAP triangle. Hotel booking across London and Mumbai. Insisting on consistency means London must reach Mumbai before confirming Martin's booking — if the link breaks, nobody can book. Making Mumbai the master for that hotel lets Pramod still book; London users can read (possibly stale) but not book. Accepting bookings on both sides keeps availability but risks double-booking the last room — which a hotel may tolerate, since it overbooks for no-shows anyway. The classic case is Dynamo's shopping cart : always writable; divergent carts are merged at checkout. Such decisions need domain experts . Reads are similar: a trading system cannot tolerate stale prices, a news site can serve pages minutes old. The book prefers to see the trade-off as consistency versus latency : involving more nodes improves consistency but increases response time; availability is then the limit of latency we tolerate before treating data as unavailable — which is why availability is often read as response time . BASE. A common shorthand: RDBMS = ACID, NoSQL = BASE (well… almost) . Basically Available — rather than enforcing immediate consistency, data is spread and replicated across the nodes so it stays available. Soft state — without immediate consistency, values may change over time; consistency is delegated to developers. Eventually consistent — consistency is reached eventually; until then reads are possible but may not reflect reality. The book finds the acronym even more contrived than ACID, and notes that Brewer saw ACID versus BASE as a spectrum . And in terms of data models: aggregate-oriented stores lean towards BASE, while graph databases are ACID . CAP in NoSQL stores When replicas are cut off from each other, a NoSQL store either refuses writes (consistency) or accepts them on both sides and reconciles later (availability). The theorem itself is defined in Lecture 3.
