A store can run in memory and flush to disk periodically: much faster, but a crash loses updates since the last flush. Worth it for user-session state (losing it annoys less than a slow site) or high-rate telemetry . Durability can often be chosen per call. Replication durability fails when a node acknowledges an update and then fails before replicating it — e.g. a master that dies before its slaves receive the write; when it returns, its writes conflict with newer ones. The fix — the master waits for some replicas to acknowledge before acknowledging the client — slows writes and makes the cluster unavailable when slaves fail. Quorums. Consistency is not all-or-nothing: the more nodes involved, the safer. This is Lecture 3's quorum consensus with every replica weighing 1, written in NoSQL Distilled's notation. With data replicated on N nodes (the replication factor ): W > N 2 (write quorum) R + W > N (strongly consistent read) W > \frac{N}{2} \quad\text{(write quorum)} \qquad\qquad R + W > N \quad\text{(strongly consistent read)} W > 2 N ​ (write quorum) R + W > N (strongly consistent read) W nodes confirm a write, R nodes are contacted for a read, N is the replication factor — not the number of nodes in the cluster. With N = 3 , two conflicting writes cannot both get a majority of 2. If writes need W = 2 , reads must contact R = 2 ; if writes are confirmed by W = 1 , reads must contact all R = 3 — strongly consistent reads even without strongly consistent writes. For fast reads you can use N = 3, W = 3, R = 1 : slow writes that fail if any node is down. A replication factor of 3 is usually enough: one node can fail while both quorums still hold. With master-slave replication you avoid conflicts more simply: write to and read from the master. Show solution Mark as read Common mistakes Common mistakes Mark difficult “NoSQL means no transactions” Aggregate-oriented stores update a single aggregate atomically, and graph databases support ACID. What they lack is atomicity across aggregates. “Schemaless means no schema” The schema moves into the application code as an implicit schema — and the database can no longer validate it. Drawing aggregate boundaries by the data alone Boundaries come from how the data is accessed . The same orders can be separate aggregates in one application and embedded in the customer in another. Reading CAP as “pick any two” A cluster cannot give up partition tolerance; the choice is C versus A during a partition, and it is a spectrum — or consistency versus latency. Confusing N with the cluster size In R + W > N, N is the replication factor. A 100-node cluster may replicate each item only 3 times. Mark as read Big picture One entity, a thousand names Mark difficult How many names and descriptions are used for the same real-world entity? Start with a single city. London is written as Londres, Londra, Londyn, Lontoo, Lunnainn, ロンドン, Лондон, 伦敦 and a hundred other strings. It is also described as the capital of the UK , the host city of the IV and XIV Olympic Games , the city of the Westminster Abbey , the city of the London Eye , the city described by Charles Dickens in his novels — and identified by URIs on GeoNames, Wikipedia and DBpedia. One entity, unbounded descriptions. Now run it the other way: how many entities have the same name? A gazetteer lists London KY, London OH, London AR, London TX, London MO, London MI, London in Conecuh County AL and dozens more — and a phone book lists Jack London in Montgomery AL at two addresses with the same phone number, another in Van Buren AR, another in La Jolla CA. One string, many entities. The definition, in one line Entity resolution is deciding whether two data structures correspond to the same real-world entity. Everything else in these three lectures is about making that decision well — and cheaply enough to be useful at scale. Reason What it covers Text variations Misspellings, acronyms, transformations, abbreviations, etc. Local knowledge Each source uses different formats — a person from a publication is not described like a person from an email — and there is no global coordination for identifier assignment. Atomic similarity methods Single values — one string against another “John D. Smith” vs. “J. D. Smith”; journal names and their abbreviations 2. Records are compared field by field A record matcher applies an atomic similarity to each comparable field — Jaro for first names, edit distance for addresses, exact match for postcodes — and combines the field scores into one decision. This quadratic wall is the reason every step that follows — shingling, minhashing, banding — exists. A common metaphor. Many problems can be expressed as finding “similar” sets — finding near-neighbours in a high-dimensional space : pages with similar words, for duplicate detection and classification by topic; customers who purchased similar products, and products with similar customer sets; images with similar features, users who visited similar websites; the dual problem: movies with similar sets of fans; and entity resolution itself. Similar documents are the running example. Given a body of documents such as the Web, find pairs with a lot of text in common: mirror sites or approximate mirrors (don't show both in a search), plagiarism including large quotations, and similar news articles at many news sites (cluster articles by the same story). Blocking and hashing The way out is the idea behind every hash index: hash each item into a bucket and only compare items that land in the same bucket. Done naively — hashing on an exact field value — this is blocking , and it misses matches that disagree on the hashed field. Parts 2 and 3 build hash functions that put similar items into the same bucket on purpose. Mark as read Summary Cheat sheet Mark difficult Entity resolution decides whether two data structures correspond to the same real-world entity: identify them, decide how to merge, update the collection. Descriptions diverge through text variations (misspellings, acronyms, abbreviations…) and local knowledge (own formats, no global identifier coordination). Solutions work at four levels: atomic values, sets, inner relationships and uncertain data. Edit distance counts inserts, deletes and updates; gap distance makes abbreviations cheap; Jaro and Jaro-Winkler suit short names. Jaccard similarity is |C₁ ∩ C₂| / |C₁ ∪ C₂|; Jaccard distance is one minus it. A distance measure is non-negative, zero exactly for identical points, symmetric, and obeys the triangle inequality. Euclidean spaces have the Lᵣ norms — L₂, L₁ (Manhattan), L∞; non-Euclidean measures include Jaccard, cosine, edit and Hamming distance. Deduplication scores pairs, clusters similar records and merges each cluster — but N records give N(N−1)/2 pairs, which Parts 2 and 3 avoid. Mark as read Big picture From entities to sets Mark difficult Entity identification is based on similarity — on finding similar items. For a small number of entities of relatively small size, things are manageable. But what if there are too many entities? Then there are too many comparisons ( time ). What if the entities are too large ? Then the memory requirements explode ( space ). The approach: see entities as sets . Finding similar items is then reduced to finding similar sets. Problem expressed as finding similar sets What it is for Entity resolution Records describing the same real-world entity Pages with similar words Classification by topic, plagiarism, avoiding repetition Netflix users with similar tastes in movies Recommendation systems Dual: movies with similar sets of fans Movie classification Many data-mining problems can be expressed as finding similar sets. Similarity of documents (MMDS §3.1.2) is about character-level similarity, not similar meaning. Testing for exact duplicates is easy — compare character by character. The interesting cases share large portions of text without being identical: Plagiarism — the plagiarist may take only parts of a document, alter a few words and reorder sentences. Mirror pages — popular sites are duplicated on several hosts; each copy differs slightly (host information, links to the other mirrors). Course pages reused from year to year behave the same way. Search engines should avoid showing near-identical pages on the first page of results. Articles from the same source — one news-agency article is republished by many newspapers, each cutting paragraphs, adding material and surrounding it with its own logo, ads and links. Aggregators such as Google News want to show only one version. Collaborative filtering (MMDS §3.1.3) recommends to users what similar users liked. Amazon can call two customers similar when their sets of purchased items have high Jaccard similarity — and two items similar when their sets of buyers do. Here similarities need not be high to be significant: mirror sites may exceed 90%, but even 20% can mark customers with similar tastes. Netflix movie ratings are not binary, so the book offers three ways to turn them into sets: ignore low ratings; give each movie two elements, liked and hated ; or, for 1-to-5 stars, put a movie into a customer's bag n n n times for n n n stars and use bag similarity. The concrete goal Given a large number N N N of documents — millions or billions — find the near-duplicate pairs. Three problems stand in the way: there are too many documents to compare all pairs; documents are so large or so many that they cannot fit in main memory; and many small pieces of one document can appear out of order in another, so order matters. Finding similar sets Many data-mining problems reduce to finding sets with a large intersection relative to their union. Entity resolution, pages with similar words (topic classification, plagiarism, repetition avoidance), customers with similar purchases or users with similar tastes in movies (recommendation), and the dual — movies with similar sets of fans. Mark as read Big picture Locality-sensitive hashing Mark difficult Signatures solve the space problem but not the pairs problem. A million documents with signatures of length 250 fit in a gigabyte, yet there are still half a trillion pairs of documents; at a microsecond per comparison that is almost six days. If you genuinely need every pair's similarity, nothing can help. But usually you want only the pairs above some similarity bound — and then locality-sensitive hashing applies: hash the items many times, in a way that makes similar items far likelier to share a bucket, and only examine the candidate pairs that collide at least once. Locality-sensitive hashing focuses on pairs of signatures likely to be similar. The general idea: from the collection of all elements (signatures, here) generate a small list of candidate pairs — pairs whose similarity must be evaluated. For signature matrices: hash columns to many buckets, and make elements of the same bucket candidate pairs. Pick a similarity threshold t t t , a fraction below 1. We want columns c c c and d d d of the signature matrix M M M to be a candidate pair if and only if their signatures agree in at least a fraction t t t of the rows, i.e. M ( i , c ) = M ( i , d ) M(i, c) = M(i, d) M ( i , c ) = M ( i , d ) for at least a fraction t t t of the values of i i i . LSH only approximates that wish. False positives and false negatives A dissimilar pair that becomes a candidate is a false positive — it costs a wasted check. A similar pair that never becomes a candidate is a false negative — it is never examined, so it is lost. Tuning LSH means trading one against the other. Locality-sensitive hashing Hash items many times so that similar items are far likelier to share a bucket. Their similarity fits neither the similar-sets nor the similar-vectors model that the theory is built on, so real entity resolution adapts the idea rather than applying it verbatim. The canonical example: Company A solicited customers for Company B, then the two quarrelled over how many customers A had actually delivered. Each held about a million records with names, addresses and phone numbers — and no field saying this is a customer A provided . A trillion pairs, and no ground truth. Scoring. Each of the three fields was worth 100 points, so an exact match everywhere scored 300. Mismatches were deducted using edit distance, with the penalty growing quadratically in the distance. Public tables then softened specific cases: Bill and William were treated as differing in one letter, though their edit distance is 5. Blocking. Scoring a trillion pairs was impossible, so three crude hash functions were used: one sent records to the same bucket only when names matched exactly, one for addresses, one for phone numbers. In practice there was no hashing at all — the records were sorted three times and consecutive ties were scored. This misses any true pair that matches exactly on none of the three fields, which was accepted: a judge would not have believed such a pair anyway. Mark as read Big picture What a vector database is Mark difficult A vector database stores multidimensional points — vectors — instead of scalar values. The number of dimensions varies from a few to several thousand , depending on how detailed the data is. Its purpose is to swiftly and precisely locate and retrieve vectors based on proximity or resemblance : a search by semantic relevance rather than by exact match or fixed criteria. With a vector database you can… Similar by… Search for songs that resonate with a particular tune Melody and rhythm Find articles that align with another article Theme and perspective Identify gadgets that mirror a certain device Characteristics and reviews Exact match versus closest match A relational query asks which rows have price = 20? — every row either matches or not. A vector query asks which items are most like this one? — every item matches to some degree, and the answer is a ranking . That single change explains almost everything else on this page. Vector database A database that stores multidimensional points (vectors), not scalar values, and retrieves them by proximity or resemblance. Vectors have from a few to several thousand dimensions. Search is by semantic relevance — songs that sound alike, articles on the same theme, gadgets with similar reviews — rather than by exact match on a value. vectors Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Traditional databases organise data as tables, nodes or documents and look for exact matches. Vector databases organise data as vectors and look for the closest match using a measure of similarity — typically with Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) search, built on techniques such as hashing and graph-based search. Where do the vectors come from? Unstructured data — images, text, audio , video — has no predefined format. An embedding turns each item into a vector, a numeric code that captures its meaning — like turning a book into a short summary that still captures the main points . Embeddings are computed by a neural network trained for the task (the slides mention a GNN); for words, it places words with similar meanings close together. Once items are vectors, similar means nearby . From an item to an answer 1 Embed An embedding model maps each image, text or audio item to a vector (say 768 numbers). The slides list five challenges: Challenge Why it matters Similarity is **vague** compared to the exact match Different applications mean different things by *similar*, so the query must say how similarity is measured — and different scores give different answers Similarity is **more expensive** than exact match A comparison touches all D dimensions; brute force over N vectors costs O(DN) per query, against one key comparison for an equality predicate Vectors are **large** and may span many pages Retrieving a full vector costs more I/O than a simple attribute and strains memory Vectors have **no properties** (like tuples or nodes do) Nothing sortable or categorical to index on, so B+ trees and hash indexes on values do not apply Vectors and other data must **co-exist** Real queries mix similarity with attribute predicates (hybrid queries), and it is unclear how to do both efficiently Why not just put a B+ tree on the vectors? A B+ tree (Lecture 1) needs keys with a total order , and closeness in that order must mean closeness of the data. Sort vectors by their first dimension and two vectors that are equal in every other dimension may end up far apart. Vector indexes therefore partition the space instead — with randomisation, learned partitions or navigable graphs. Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Show answer Mark as read Core concepts Query processing: scores, query types, variants Mark difficult Query processing starts from a search specification: which score measures similarity, which kind of query , and through which interface . Score design. A similarity score f(a, b) maps two vectors to a number. The slides distinguish three kinds: Basic scores come straight from the vector space: inner product a·b, cosine (the angle, ignoring length), Minkowski distances (Euclidean L₂, Manhattan L₁ — see Lecture 2), Hamming (number of differing dimensions) and Mahalanobis . For some, larger means more similar (inner product, cosine similarity); for distances, smaller does. Combined (aggregate) scores merge several scores into one comparable number — the mean or a weighted sum — when a query or an entity has several vectors. Learned scores are fitted to the data by metric learning . Score selection is choosing the best score for a task. Each costs O(D). Query types. A database manipulation query inserts, updates or deletes vectors. A search query returns part of the collection: k-NN — the k vectors nearest to the query vector q. ANN — approximate nearest neighbours: k vectors that are almost the nearest, found much faster with an index. (c, k)-search — the slides' general form: find the k most similar vectors, none of which is more than c times worse than the best . Formally, a k-size result S′ with d(x′, q) ≤ c · min d(x, q) for every x′ in S′. Range — all vectors within a threshold r: { x | d(x, q) ≤ r }, when you want everything similar enough, not a fixed number. Answer quality is measured with precision and recall against the exact answer. The basic operator is similarity projection : project every vector onto its score against q, then sort or keep a top-k priority queue. Query variants. Hybrid (predicated, filtered ) queries: each vector has structured attributes, and every result must also satisfy a boolean predicate — the k most similar items with price < 100 . Common in e-commerce recommendation. Multi-vector queries: the query, each entity, or both have several vectors — a face photographed from several angles — compared through an aggregate score . Batched queries: many searches arrive at once and can share work, which suits GPUs. A hybrid query can be run in three ways: pre-filtering (apply the predicate first, then search what remains — a block-first scan), post-filtering (search first, then drop failing results — which can return fewer than k ) or single-stage filtering (check the predicate while traversing the index — a visit-first scan). Similarity score A function f(a, b) mapping two vectors to a number. Basic scores: inner product, cosine, Minkowski (Euclidean, Manhattan), Hamming, Mahalanobis. Combined (aggregate) scores such as the mean or a weighted sum merge several scores into one, for entities with several vectors. Learned scores come from metric learning. Mark as read Core concepts Indexing: table, tree and graph Mark difficult An index speeds up search by partitioning the collection so that most vectors are never compared. Since vectors cannot be sorted, vector indexes partition with randomisation , learned partitioning or navigable partitioning , and by structure they are table-based , tree-based or graph-based . Family Idea Examples Trade-off Table-based: **LSH** Random hash functions put similar vectors in the same bucket; the query is hashed and colliding vectors are candidates E2LSH (random hyperplanes), FALCONN Easy to update; error guarantees; big buckets help recall but are slow to scan Table-based: **Learning to hash (L2H)** Machine learning learns the hash function, e.g. k-means clusters as buckets SPANN, spectral hashing High-quality partitions, but data-dependent: poor with out-of-distribution updates Table-based: **Quantization** Map vectors to **smaller vectors** or codes to save space and comparison time SQ (64 → 32 bits per dimension), PQ (product quantization), IVF-PQ / IVFADC Compression loses some accuracy **Tree-based** Recursively partition the vectors to build a search tree k-d tree, PCA trees, random-projection trees, ANNOY (forest of trees) Logarithmic search; deterministic splits adapt poorly to high dimensions **Graph-based**: KNN graphs Each vector is connected to its k most similar vectors — edges for close similarity KGraph (NN-Descent), EFANNA Exact O(N²) construction; answered by walking the graph **Graph-based**: MSNs and small-world graphs Edges chosen to make the graph **easy to navigate**: greedy best-first search reaches the target in about O(log N) steps NSG, Vamana/DiskANN, NSW, **HNSW** Very fast in practice, less theory, hard to update The slides' classification of vector indexes (SIGMOD tutorial, Section 2.2). MSN = monotonic search network. LSH, again. Lecture 6 used LSH to find similar documents: split minhash signatures into b bands of r rows and make every pair that agrees in a whole band a candidate. A vector LSH index is the same construction: each vector is hashed into L tables , each hash the concatenation of K functions from a locality-sensitive family (for vectors: random hyperplanes or projections instead of minhashes). L plays the role of b, K the role of r, and the same S-curve trade-off between false positives and false negatives applies. Quantization in one picture: product quantization splits a 128-dimensional vector into, say, 8 sub-vectors of 16 dimensions, runs k-means (Lecture 4) separately in each sub-space with 256 centroids, and stores each sub-vector as the one-byte id of its nearest centroid — 8 bytes instead of 512. Graph search in one picture: start at an entry node, look at its neighbours, move to the one closest to q, and repeat until no neighbour is closer. HNSW stacks such graphs in layers, sparse at the top and dense at the bottom, like a skip list, so the walk takes long jumps first and fine steps last. Two different kinds of graph A graph-based vector index is a navigation structure over vectors built by the vector database — not a graph database like Neo4j (Lecture 11). Weaviate does offer a graph data model over its entities as well, but that is a separate feature. Executing at scale. Many vector databases are distributed : the collection is sharded and replicated (Lecture 3) and a search is scatter-gather — every shard returns its local top k and a coordinator merges them. Shards can be equal-sized or index-guided (all vectors of one bucket in one shard). Search is accelerated with SIMD and GPUs . Because many indexes are hard to update, systems apply updates out of place — asynchronously on replicas, in a buffer merged in bulk later, or in a log-structured merge (LSM) tree. Vector index A structure that partitions a vector collection so it can be searched without comparing every vector: table-based, tree-based or graph-based. Vectors have no natural sort order or categories, so B+ trees and hash indexes on values do not apply. Vector indexes use randomisation (LSH), learned partitioning (learning to hash, k-means) and navigable partitioning (graphs) instead. indexing Quantization Compression that maps each vector to a smaller vector or code, cutting storage and comparison cost at some loss of accuracy. Scalar quantization shrinks every dimension (e.g. 64 → 32 bits); product quantization splits the space into sub-spaces and replaces each part with the id of its nearest k-means centroid. IVF variants first bucket vectors by k-means cluster. indexing Graph-based vector index A graph over the vectors, with edges between similar ones; a search walks greedily from node to node towards the query. A k-nearest-neighbour graph (KNNG) connects each vector to its k most similar ones. Monotonic search networks (MSNs) and small-world graphs (SWGs) choose edges that make the graph easy to navigate; HNSW adds layers like a skip list. Fast in practice, but hard to update. indexing Memory cards Answer in your head first, then flip the card. Three structural families of vector indexes? Show answer What does quantization do? Show answer Mark as read Common mistakes Common mistakes Mark difficult Expecting exact answers by default Most vector searches are approximate (ANN): faster, but the result can miss some true nearest neighbours. Quality is measured by recall. Treating all scores as interchangeable Cosine ignores length, the inner product rewards it, Euclidean measures position. The same collection gives different rankings — score selection matters. Forgetting that post-filtering can return fewer than k Filtering after the search drops results; pre-filtering or single-stage filtering keeps k. Indexing vectors with a B+ tree Vectors have no meaningful total order; vector indexes partition the space with hashing, trees of splits or navigable graphs. Confusing a graph-based index with a graph database HNSW is a navigation structure over vectors, not a property graph you query with Cypher. Calling Faiss a database Faiss is a library for similarity search; it has no multi-user support, storage management or query language. Mark as read Summary Cheat sheet Mark difficult A vector database stores multidimensional points (a few to several thousand dimensions) and retrieves them by proximity: semantic relevance, not exact match. Embeddings, computed by a neural network, turn images, text and audio into vectors that summarise their main points; similar items get nearby vectors. Applications: retail recommendation, financial analysis, healthcare, NLP and LLM retrieval, media analysis, anomaly detection. Challenges: similarity is vague and expensive, vectors are large (may span pages), have no sortable properties to index, and must co-exist with other data. Scores are basic (cosine, inner product, Euclidean, Hamming…), combined (mean or weighted sum of several) or learned (metric learning); picking the right one is score selection. (c, k)-search returns k vectors no more than c times worse than the best: c = 1 is exact k-NN, c > 1 is ANN. Range queries use a threshold instead of k. Hybrid queries add attribute predicates (pre-filter, post-filter or filter during the search); multi-vector queries combine several vectors per entity with an aggregate score. Indexes: table-based (LSH, learning to hash, quantization), tree-based (recursive partitioning, ANNOY) and graph-based (KNN graphs, navigable small-world graphs such as HNSW).
